questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wheel revolves about its axis with a uniform angular acceleration. Beginning from rest, it attains $100 \text{ rev/sec}$ in $4$ seconds. Determine the angular acceleration and the angle rotated during these four seconds.
questions.solution:
Initial angular velocity, $\omega_0 = 0$

Final angular velocity, $\omega = 100 \text{ rev/s}$

Time, $t = 4 \text{ s}$

Using the first equation of rotational motion, $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$

$100 = 0 + \alpha (4) \Rightarrow \alpha = 25 \text{ rev/s}^2$

Using the second equation of rotational motion, $\theta = \omega_0 t + \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$

$\theta = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}(25)(4)^2 = 200 \text{ rev}$

Converting revolutions to radians:

$\theta = 200 \times 2\pi = 400\pi \text{ rad}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Starting from rest, a wheel is uniformly accelerated at $4 \text{ rad/s}^2$ for $10$ seconds. Subsequently, it rotates uniformly for the next $10$ seconds, and is finally brought to rest over the following $10$ seconds. Determine the total angle rotated by the wheel.
questions.solution:
The motion of the wheel can be divided into three phases.

In the first phase, the wheel starts from rest and accelerates uniformly.
Initial angular velocity, $\omega_0 = 0$
Angular acceleration, $\alpha_1 = 4 \text{ rad/s}^2$
Time, $t_1 = 10 \text{ s}$
Angle rotated, $\theta_1 = \omega_0 t_1 + \dfrac{1}{2} \alpha_1 t_1^2 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times (10)^2 = 200 \text{ rad}$
Angular velocity at the end of this phase, $\omega_1 = \omega_0 + \alpha_1 t_1 = 0 + 4 \times 10 = 40 \text{ rad/s}$

In the second phase, the wheel rotates uniformly.
Angular velocity, $\omega_1 = 40 \text{ rad/s}$
Time, $t_2 = 10 \text{ s}$
Angle rotated, $\theta_2 = \omega_1 t_2 = 40 \times 10 = 400 \text{ rad}$

In the third phase, the wheel is brought to rest uniformly.
Initial angular velocity, $\omega_1 = 40 \text{ rad/s}$
Final angular velocity, $\omega_2 = 0$
Time, $t_3 = 10 \text{ s}$
Angle rotated, $\theta_3 = \left( \dfrac{\omega_1 + \omega_2}{2} \right) t_3 = \left( \dfrac{40 + 0}{2} \right) \times 10 = 200 \text{ rad}$

Total angle rotated by the wheel is $\theta = \theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_3 = 200 + 400 + 200 = 800 \text{ rad}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the angular velocity of a body rotating with an acceleration of $2 \text{ rev/s}^2$ as it completes the $5$th revolution after starting.
questions.solution:
Given:
Initial angular velocity, $\omega_0 = 0$
Angular acceleration, $\alpha = 2 \text{ rev/s}^2$
Angular displacement, $\theta = 5 \text{ rev}$

Using the equation of rotational kinematics:
$\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$

Substituting the given values:
$\omega^2 = 0^2 + 2(2)(5)$
$\omega^2 = 20$
$\omega = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5} \text{ rev/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body rotates about a fixed axis with an angular acceleration of one $\text{radian/second/second}$. Determine the angle through which it rotates during the time in which its angular velocity increases from $5 \text{ rad/s}$ to $15 \text{ rad/s}$.
questions.solution:
Using the third equation of rotational kinematics:

$\omega_f^2 = \omega_i^2 + 2\alpha\theta$

Given $\omega_i = 5 \text{ rad/s}$, $\omega_f = 15 \text{ rad/s}$, and $\alpha = 1 \text{ rad/s}^2$.

Substituting the values into the equation:

$(15)^2 = (5)^2 + 2(1)\theta$

$225 = 25 + 2\theta$

$2\theta = 200$

$\theta = 100 \text{ rad}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A disc of radius $10 \text{ cm}$ rotates about its axis with an angular speed of $20 \text{ rad/s}$. Determine the linear speed of a point situated on the rim.
questions.solution:
Given the radius of the disc, $r = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$

Angular speed, $\omega = 20 \text{ rad/s}$

The linear speed $v$ of a point situated on the rim is given by the relation:

$v = r\omega$

Substituting the given values:

$v = 0.1 \times 20 = 2 \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A disc of radius $10 \text{ cm}$ rotates about its axis with an angular speed of $20 \text{ rad/s}$. Determine the linear speed of the middle point of a radius.
questions.solution:
Given radius of the disc, $R = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$

Angular speed, $\omega = 20 \text{ rad/s}$

Distance of the middle point of the radius from the axis of rotation, $r = \dfrac{R}{2} = \dfrac{0.1}{2} = 0.05 \text{ m}$

Linear speed is given by $v = r\omega$

$v = 0.05 \times 20 = 1 \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A disc rotates about its axis with a uniform angular acceleration of $4 \text{ rad/s}^2$. Determine the radial and tangential accelerations of a particle located $1 \text{ cm}$ from the axis at the end of the first second after the disc begins rotating.
questions.solution:
Given initial angular velocity $\omega_0 = 0$ and angular acceleration $\alpha = 4 \text{ rad/s}^2$.

The angular velocity at time $t = 1 \text{ s}$ is given by:

$\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t = 0 + 4 \times 1 = 4 \text{ rad/s}$

The radial acceleration $a_r$ of a particle at a distance $r = 1 \text{ cm}$ from the axis is:

$a_r = \omega^2 r = (4)^2 \times 1 = 16 \text{ cm/s}^2$

The tangential acceleration $a_t$ of the particle is:

$a_t = \alpha r = 4 \times 1 = 4 \text{ cm/s}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block is suspended from a string wrapped on a disc of radius $20 \text{ cm}$, which is free to rotate about its fixed horizontal axis. If the angular speed of the disc is $10 \text{ rad/s}$ at a particular instant, at what speed is the block descending at that instant?
questions.solution:
Given, radius of the disc, $R = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$

Angular speed of the disc, $\omega = 10 \text{ rad/s}$

The speed of the descending block is equal to the tangential speed of the points on the rim of the disc.

$v = R \omega$

$v = 0.2 \times 10 = 2 \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three particles, each having a mass of $200 \text{ g}$, are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle with a side length of $10 \text{ cm}$. Determine the moment of inertia of the system about an axis passing through one of the particles and perpendicular to the plane of the particles.
questions.solution:
Let the three particles be placed at the vertices A, B, and C of the equilateral triangle.

Mass of each particle, $m = 200 \text{ g} = 0.2 \text{ kg}$

Side length of the triangle, $a = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$

The axis of rotation passes through one of the particles (say, at vertex A) and is perpendicular to the plane of the triangle.

The perpendicular distance of the particle at A from the axis is $r_A = 0$.

The perpendicular distances of the particles at B and C from the axis are $r_B = a$ and $r_C = a$.

The moment of inertia of the system about the given axis is:

$I = m r_A^2 + m r_B^2 + m r_C^2$

$I = m(0)^2 + m(a)^2 + m(a)^2$

$I = 2ma^2$

Substituting the given values:

$I = 2 \times 0.2 \times (0.1)^2$

$I = 0.4 \times 0.01 = 0.004 \text{ kg-m}^2$

$I = 4.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg-m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three particles, each having a mass of $200 \text{ g}$, are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle with a side length of $10 \text{ cm}$. Determine the moment of inertia of the system about an axis joining two of the particles.
questions.solution:
Let the three particles be A, B, and C, each of mass $m = 200 \text{ g} = 0.2 \text{ kg}$.

Side length of the equilateral triangle, $a = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$.

Let the axis of rotation pass through particles A and B. The perpendicular distances of particles A and B from the axis are zero ($r_A = 0$, $r_B = 0$).

The perpendicular distance of particle C from the axis AB is the altitude of the equilateral triangle:

$r_C = a \sin 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a$

The moment of inertia of the system about the axis AB is given by:

$I = m_A r_A^2 + m_B r_B^2 + m_C r_C^2$

$I = m(0)^2 + m(0)^2 + m \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a \right)^2$

$I = \dfrac{3}{4} m a^2$

Substituting the given values:

$I = \dfrac{3}{4} \times 0.2 \times (0.1)^2$

$I = \dfrac{3}{4} \times 0.2 \times 0.01$

$I = 0.15 \times 0.01 = 1.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg-m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the moment of inertia of a pair of spheres, each possessing a mass $m$ and radius $r$, placed in contact, about the tangent passing through their point of contact.
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a solid sphere of mass $m$ and radius $r$ about its diameter is given by $I_{cm} = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2$.

The tangent passing through the point of contact of the two spheres is at a perpendicular distance $r$ from the center of each sphere.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of one sphere about this tangent is $I_1 = I_{cm} + mr^2 = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2 + mr^2 = \dfrac{7}{5}mr^2$.

Since the system consists of two identical spheres, the total moment of inertia of the pair about the common tangent is $I = I_1 + I_2 = \dfrac{7}{5}mr^2 + \dfrac{7}{5}mr^2 = \dfrac{14}{5}mr^2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Particles having masses of $1 \text{ g}$, $2 \text{ g}$, $3 \text{ g}$, ..., $100 \text{ g}$ are placed at the marks $1 \text{ cm}$, $2 \text{ cm}$, $3 \text{ cm}$, ..., $100 \text{ cm}$ respectively on a metre scale. Determine the moment of inertia of this system of particles about the perpendicular bisector of the metre scale.
questions.solution:
The perpendicular bisector of a metre scale passes through its midpoint at $50 \text{ cm}$.

The moment of inertia of the system about this axis is given by:

$I = \sum_{i=1}^{100} m_i r_i^2$

where $m_i = i \text{ g}$ and the distance from the axis is $r_i = |i - 50| \text{ cm}$.

$I = \sum_{i=1}^{100} i (i - 50)^2$

Let $j = i - 50$. As $i$ varies from $1$ to $100$, $j$ varies from $-49$ to $50$.

$I = \sum_{j=-49}^{50} (j + 50) j^2 = \sum_{j=-49}^{50} j^3 + 50 \sum_{j=-49}^{50} j^2$

Since $j^3$ is an odd power, the sum of symmetric terms is zero, giving $\sum_{j=-49}^{49} j^3 = 0$.

$\sum_{j=-49}^{50} j^3 = 50^3 = 125000$

For the second term, using the sum of squares formula $\sum_{j=1}^{n} j^2 = \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$:

$\sum_{j=-49}^{50} j^2 = 50^2 + 2 \sum_{j=1}^{49} j^2$

$\sum_{j=1}^{49} j^2 = \dfrac{49 \times 50 \times 99}{6} = 40425$

$\sum_{j=-49}^{50} j^2 = 2500 + 2(40425) = 83350$

Substituting these values back into the equation for $I$:

$I = 125000 + 50(83350) = 125000 + 4167500 = 4292500 \text{ g cm}^2$

Converting the units to $\text{kg m}^2$:

$I = 4292500 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg} \times (10^{-2} \text{ m})^2$

$I = 4292500 \times 10^{-7} \text{ kg m}^2 = 0.42925 \text{ kg m}^2$

Rounding to two decimal places, we get $0.43 \text{ kg m}^2$.

Answer: $0.43 \text{ kg m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod with a mass of $0.50 \text{ kg}$ and a length of $1 \text{ m}$ has a moment of inertia of $0.10 \text{ kg-m}^2$ about an axis perpendicular to it. Determine the distance from this axis to the middle point of the rod.
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about an axis passing through its center of mass and perpendicular to its length is given by:

$I_{cm} = \dfrac{mL^2}{12}$

Substituting the given values $m = 0.50 \text{ kg}$ and $L = 1 \text{ m}$:

$I_{cm} = \dfrac{0.50 \times (1)^2}{12} = \dfrac{1}{24} \text{ kg-m}^2$

According to the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia $I$ about any parallel axis is:

$I = I_{cm} + md^2$

where $d$ is the distance from the axis to the center of mass (middle point) of the rod.

Given $I = 0.10 \text{ kg-m}^2$, substituting the values gives:

$0.10 = \dfrac{1}{24} + 0.50 \times d^2$

$\dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{24} = \dfrac{1}{2} d^2$

$\dfrac{12 - 5}{120} = \dfrac{1}{2} d^2$

$\dfrac{7}{120} = \dfrac{1}{2} d^2$

$d^2 = \dfrac{7}{60} \approx 0.1167 \text{ m}^2$

$d = \sqrt{0.1167} \approx 0.34 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the radius of gyration of a circular ring of radius $r$ about a line perpendicular to the ring's plane and passing through one of its particles.
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a circular ring of mass $M$ and radius $r$ about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is $I_{cm} = M r^2$.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of the ring about an axis passing through a particle on its circumference and perpendicular to its plane is given by:

$I = I_{cm} + M d^2$

Here, the distance between the parallel axes is $d = r$.

$I = M r^2 + M r^2 = 2 M r^2$

The radius of gyration $k$ is defined by $I = M k^2$. Equating the two expressions for $I$:

$M k^2 = 2 M r^2$

$k^2 = 2 r^2$

$k = \sqrt{2}\,r$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform disc has a radius of gyration equal to its radius $r$ about a line perpendicular to the disc. Determine the distance of this line from the centre.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the uniform disc be $M$ and its radius be $r$.

The moment of inertia of the disc about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is $I_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{2} M r^2$.

Let the required axis be at a distance $d$ from the centre. By the theorem of parallel axes, the moment of inertia about this axis is:

$I = I_{cm} + M d^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} M r^2 + M d^2$

The radius of gyration $k$ about this axis is given as $r$. Therefore, the moment of inertia can also be written as:

$I = M k^2 = M r^2$

Equating the two expressions for $I$:

$\dfrac{1}{2} M r^2 + M d^2 = M r^2$

$M d^2 = M r^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} M r^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} M r^2$

$d^2 = \dfrac{r^2}{2}$

$d = \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the moment of inertia of a uniform square plate having mass $m$ and edge $a$ about one of its diagonals.
questions.solution:
Let the square plate lie in the $xy$-plane with its center at the origin and its edges parallel to the $x$ and $y$ axes.

The moment of inertia of the square plate about the $x$-axis passing through its center is $I_x = \dfrac{ma^2}{12}$.

The moment of inertia of the square plate about the $y$-axis passing through its center is $I_y = \dfrac{ma^2}{12}$.

By the perpendicular axis theorem, the moment of inertia about the $z$-axis passing through the center and perpendicular to the plane is $I_z = I_x + I_y = \dfrac{ma^2}{12} + \dfrac{ma^2}{12} = \dfrac{ma^2}{6}$.

Let the two diagonals of the square plate be the $x'$ and $y'$ axes. Since the diagonals are perpendicular to each other and lie in the plane of the plate, we can apply the perpendicular axis theorem again.

By symmetry, the moment of inertia about both diagonals is the same, so $I_{x'} = I_{y'}$.

Using the perpendicular axis theorem, $I_z = I_{x'} + I_{y'} = 2I_{x'}$.

Substituting the value of $I_z$, we get $2I_{x'} = \dfrac{ma^2}{6}$.

$I_{x'} = \dfrac{ma^2}{12}$.

Thus, the moment of inertia of the square plate about one of its diagonals is $\dfrac{ma^2}{12}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The surface density (mass/area) of a circular disc having a radius $a$ varies with the distance from the centre according to $\rho(r) = A + Br$. Determine its moment of inertia about a line passing through its centre and perpendicular to the plane of the disc.
questions.solution:
Consider an elemental ring of radius $r$ and thickness $dr$ in the circular disc.

The area of this elemental ring is $dA = 2\pi r dr$.

The mass of the elemental ring is $dm = \rho(r) dA = (A + Br) 2\pi r dr$.

The moment of inertia of this elemental ring about the axis passing through the centre and perpendicular to the plane is $dI = r^2 dm$.

Substituting the expression for $dm$:

$dI = r^2 (A + Br) 2\pi r dr$

$dI = 2\pi (A r^3 + B r^4) dr$

The total moment of inertia of the disc is obtained by integrating $dI$ from $r = 0$ to $r = a$:

$I = \int_{0}^{a} 2\pi (A r^3 + B r^4) dr$

$I = 2\pi \left[ \dfrac{A r^4}{4} + \dfrac{B r^5}{5} \right]_{0}^{a}$

$I = 2\pi \left[ $\dfrac{A a^4}{4} + \dfrac{B a^5}{5} \right]

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ is launched with a speed $u$ at an angle $\theta$ relative to the horizontal. Determine the magnitude of the torque of the particle's weight about the point of projection when the particle reaches its highest point.
questions.solution:
At the highest point of the trajectory, the horizontal distance of the particle from the point of projection is half of the horizontal range, i.e., $x = \dfrac{R}{2}$.

The horizontal range is given by $R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g} = \dfrac{2 u^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta}{g}$.

Thus, $x = \dfrac{u^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta}{g}$.

The force acting on the particle is its weight, $F = mg$, which acts vertically downwards.

The magnitude of the torque of the weight about the point of projection is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force.

$\tau = F \times x = mg \times $\$left(\dfrac{u^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta}{g}\right)

$\tau = m u^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A simple pendulum of length $l$ is displaced to form an angle $	heta$ with the vertical. Calculate the magnitude of the torque exerted by the weight $w$ of the bob about the point of suspension, and state when this torque is zero.
options: $wl\cos\theta$, when the bob is at the lowest point
$wl\sin\theta$, when the bob is at an extreme position
$wl\sin\theta$, when the bob is at the lowest point
$wl\cos\theta$, when the bob is at an extreme position
questions.solution:
The torque about the point of suspension is given by the cross product of the position vector $\vec{r}$ and the force $\vec{F}$.

Here, the force is the weight $w$ acting vertically downwards, and the magnitude of the position vector is the length of the pendulum $l$.

The angle between the position vector and the force vector is $\theta$.

The magnitude of the torque is $\tau = |\vec{r} \times \vec{F}| = l w \sin\theta$.

The torque is zero when $\tau = 0$, which implies $\sin\theta = 0$, giving $\theta = 0$.

This condition corresponds to the bob being at its lowest point.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A force of $6.0 \text{ N}$ applied at $30^\circ$ to a wrench at a distance of $8 \text{ cm}$ from the nut is just sufficient to loosen the nut. Determine the force $F$ that would be required to loosen it if it acts perpendicularly to the wrench at a distance of $16 \text{ cm}$ from the nut.
questions.solution:
The torque required to loosen the nut remains constant in both cases.

The torque $\tau$ produced by a force is given by $\tau = r F \sin \theta$.

For the first case:
$F_1 = 6.0 \text{ N}$
$r_1 = 8 \text{ cm}$
$\theta_1 = 30^\circ$
$\tau_1 = 8 \times 6.0 \times \sin 30^\circ = 48 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 24 \text{ N cm}$

For the second case:
$F_2 = F$
$r_2 = 16 \text{ cm}$
$\theta_2 = 90^\circ$
$\tau_2 = 16 \times F \times \sin 90^\circ = 16F \text{ N cm}$

Equating the torques:
$\tau_1 = \tau_2$
$24 = 16F$
$F = \dfrac{24}{16} = 1.5 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cubical block of mass $m$ and edge length $a$ is sliding down a rough inclined plane of inclination $	heta$ at a uniform speed. Determine the torque of the normal force exerted on the block about its centre.
questions.solution:
Since the block is sliding down the inclined plane at a uniform speed, its net acceleration and net angular acceleration are zero.

The forces acting on the block are its weight $mg$, the normal force $N$, and the frictional force $f$.

For translational equilibrium along the inclined plane:

$f = mg \sin\theta$

The block is in rotational equilibrium, so the net torque about its centre of mass must be zero. The weight $mg$ passes through the centre of mass, so its torque is zero.

The frictional force $f$ acts along the bottom surface of the block, which is at a perpendicular distance of $\dfrac{a}{2}$ from the centre of mass. The torque due to friction about the centre is:

$\tau_f = f \times \dfrac{a}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}mga \sin\theta$

To maintain rotational equilibrium, the torque due to the normal force $\tau_N$ about the centre must be equal and opposite to the torque due to friction.

$\tau_N = \tau_f = \dfrac{1}{2}mga \sin\theta$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A square plate having a mass of $120 \text{ g}$ and an edge of $5.0 \text{ cm}$ rotates about one of its edges. Determine the torque acting on the plate if it undergoes a uniform angular acceleration of $0.2 \text{ rad/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a square plate of mass $m$ and side length $a$ about one of its edges is given by:

$I = \dfrac{m a^2}{3}$

Given:

$m = 120 \text{ g} = 0.12 \text{ kg}$

$a = 5.0 \text{ cm} = 0.05 \text{ m}$

Substituting the values:

$I = \dfrac{0.12 \times (0.05)^2}{3}$

$I = 0.04 \times 0.0025 = 1.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ kg m}^2$

The torque $\tau$ is given by:

$\tau = I \alpha$

Given $\alpha = 0.2 \text{ rad/s}^2$:

$\tau = (1.0 \times 10^{-4}) \times 0.2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ N m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A horizontal rod of mass $m$ and length $L$ is free to rotate about a vertical axis passing through its centre. A constant horizontal force of magnitude $F$ acts on the rod at a distance of $L/4$ from the centre. The force remains perpendicular to the rod at all times. Determine the angle rotated by the rod in time $t$ after the motion begins.
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of the rod about the vertical axis passing through its centre is $I = \dfrac{mL^2}{12}$.

The torque acting on the rod due to the force $F$ applied at a distance of $L/4$ from the centre and always perpendicular to the rod is $\tau = F \times \dfrac{L}{4}$.

Using the relation $\tau = I\alpha$, the angular acceleration $\alpha$ is given by:

$\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I} = \dfrac{\dfrac{FL}{4}}{\dfrac{mL^2}{12}} = \dfrac{3F}{mL}$

Since the rod starts from rest, the angle rotated in time $t$ is:

$\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3F}{mL}\right)t^2 = \dfrac{3Ft^2}{2mL}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A square plate of mass $120 ext{ g}$ and edge $5.0 ext{ cm}$ has a uniform angular acceleration of $0.2 ext{ rad/s}^2$. Calculate the torque on the plate if it rotates about a diagonal with the same angular acceleration.
questions.solution: For a square lamina, the moment of inertia about any axis in its plane through the center is $I = \dfrac{1}{12} m a^2$. Here $m = 0.12 \text{ kg}$ and $a = 0.05 \text{ m}$. Thus $I = \dfrac{1}{12}(0.12)(0.05^2) = 2.5 \times 10^{-5} \text{ kg m}^2$. The torque is $\tau = I\alpha = (2.5 \times 10^{-5})(0.2) = 5.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ N m}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A flywheel with a moment of inertia of $5.0 \text{ kg-m}^2$ is rotated at a speed of $60 \text{ rad/s}$. Due to friction at the axle, it comes to rest in $5.0 \text{ minutes}$. Determine the average torque of the friction.
questions.solution:
Given moment of inertia, $I = 5.0 \text{ kg-m}^2$

questions.q: A flywheel with a moment of inertia of $5.0 \text{ kg-m}^2$ is rotated at a speed of $60 \text{ rad/s}$. Due to friction at the axle, it comes to rest in $5.0 \text{ minutes}$. Determine the total work done by the friction.
questions.solution:
Initial kinetic energy of the flywheel is given by $K_i = \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega_i^2$.

Substituting the given values, $I = 5.0 \text{ kg-m}^2$ and $\omega_i = 60 \text{ rad/s}$:

$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5.0 \times (60)^2$

$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5.0 \times 3600 = 9000 \text{ J}$

Final kinetic energy $K_f = 0$ since the flywheel comes to rest.

According to the work-energy theorem, the total work done by friction is equal to the change in kinetic energy:

$W = K_f - K_i = 0 - 9000 \text{ J} = -9000 \text{ J}$

The magnitude of the total work done by friction is $9.0 \text{ kJ}$.

questions.solution:
Initial angular velocity, $\omega_0 = 60 \text{ rad/s}$

Time taken to come to rest, $t = 5.0 \text{ minutes} = 300 \text{ s}$

Final angular velocity, $\omega = 0$

Using the first equation of rotational motion, $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$

$0 = 60 + \alpha (300)$

$\alpha = -\dfrac{60}{300} = -0.2 \text{ rad/s}^2$

We need to find the angular momentum $1 \text{ minute}$ ($60 \text{ s}$) before it stops. The time elapsed from the start is $t' = 5.0 - 1.0 = 4.0 \text{ minutes} = 240 \text{ s}$.

Angular velocity at $t' = 240 \text{ s}$ is given by:

$\omega' = \omega_0 + \alpha t'$

$\omega' = 60 + (-0.2)(240) = 60 - 48 = 12 \text{ rad/s}$

Angular momentum at this instant is:

$L = I\omega'$

$L = 5.0 \times 12 = 60 \text{ kg-m}^2/\text{s}$

questions.q: A cylinder rotating at an angular speed of $50 \text{ rev/s}$ is brought into contact with an identical stationary cylinder. Due to kinetic friction, torques act on the two cylinders, accelerating the stationary one and decelerating the moving one. If the common magnitude of the acceleration and deceleration is $1 \text{ rev/s}^2$, how much time will it take before the two cylinders attain equal angular speed?
questions.solution:
Let the initial angular speed of the first cylinder be $\omega_1 = 50 \text{ rev/s}$ and the second cylinder be $\omega_2 = 0$.

The angular deceleration of the first cylinder is $\alpha_1 = 1 \text{ rev/s}^2$ and the angular acceleration of the second cylinder is $\alpha_2 = 1 \text{ rev/s}^2$.

Let $t$ be the time taken for the two cylinders to attain equal angular speed $\omega$.

Using the first equation of rotational motion for both cylinders:

For the first cylinder: $\omega = \omega_1 - \alpha_1 t = 50 - t$

For the second cylinder: $\omega = \omega_2 + \alpha_2 t = 0 + t$

Equating the final angular speeds:

$50 - t = t$

$2t = 50$

$t = 25 \text{ s}$

questions.q: A wheel of mass $10 \text{ kg}$ and radius $20 \text{ cm}$ is spinning at an angular speed of $100 \text{ rev/min}$ when the motor is switched off. Ignoring friction at the axle, determine the force that must be applied tangentially to the wheel to bring it to a halt in $10$ revolutions.
questions.solution:
Given the initial angular speed of the wheel:

$\omega_0 = 100 \text{ rev/min} = 100 \times \dfrac{2\pi}{60} = \dfrac{10\pi}{3} \text{ rad/s}$

The final angular speed is $\omega = 0$.

The angular displacement to bring the wheel to a halt is:

$\theta = 10 \text{ rev} = 10 \times 2\pi = 20\pi \text{ rad}$

Using the kinematic equation for rotational motion:

$\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$

Substituting the values:

$0 = \left(\dfrac{10\pi}{3}\right)^2 + 2\alpha(20\pi)$

$0 = \dfrac{100\pi^2}{9} + 40\pi\alpha$

$\alpha = -\dfrac{100\pi^2}{9 \times 40\pi} = -\dfrac{5\pi}{18} \text{ rad/s}^2$

Assuming the wheel to be a solid disc, its moment of inertia is:

$I = \dfrac{1}{2}mR^2$

The magnitude of the required torque is:

$\tau = I|\alpha| = $\$left(\dfrac{1}{2}$mR^2\right) \$left(\dfrac{5\pi}{18}\right)

Since the torque is provided by a tangential force $F$, we have $\tau = F \times R$. Therefore:

$F \times R = $\dfrac{1}{2}$mR^2 \times $\dfrac{5\pi}{18}

$F = $\dfrac{1}{2}$mR \times $\dfrac{5\pi}{18}

Substituting $m = 10 \text{ kg}$ and $R = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$:

$F = $\dfrac{1}{2} \times$10 \times 0.2 \times $\dfrac{5\pi}{18}

$F = 1 \times $\dfrac{5\pi}{18} = \dfrac{5\pi}{18} \text{ N}

$F \approx $\dfrac{5 \times 3.1416}{18} \approx$0.87 \text{ N}$

Answer: $0.87 \text{ N}

questions.q: A body rotating at $20 \text{ rad/s}$ is subjected to a constant torque that provides a deceleration of $2 \text{ rad/s}^2$. If the torque continues to act, at what time will the body possess a kinetic energy equal to its initial value?
questions.solution:
The initial kinetic energy of the rotating body is given by $K_i = \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega_0^2$.

For the body to possess a kinetic energy equal to its initial value at a later time $t > 0$, its final angular velocity must be $\omega = -\omega_0$.

Given $\omega_0 = 20 \text{ rad/s}$ and angular deceleration $\alpha = -2 \text{ rad/s}^2$, we have $\omega = -20 \text{ rad/s}$.

Using the first equation of rotational kinematics:

$\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$

$-20 = 20 - 2t$

$2t = 40$

$t = 20 \text{ s}$

questions.q: A light rod of length $1\text{ m}$ is pivoted at its centre, with two masses of $5\text{ kg}$ and $2\text{ kg}$ suspended from its ends, as shown in the figure. Determine the initial angular acceleration of the rod, assuming it is horizontal at the beginning.
questions.solution:
Let the length of the rod be $L = 1\text{ m}$. Since the rod is pivoted at its centre, the distance of each mass from the pivot is $r = \dfrac{L}{2} = 0.5\text{ m}$.

The forces acting on the system are the weights of the two masses. The net torque $\tau$ about the pivot is the difference between the torques produced by the $5\text{ kg}$ and $2\text{ kg}$ masses:

$\tau = m_1 g r - m_2 g r = (m_1 - m_2) g r$

Substituting the given values (taking $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$):

$\tau = (5 - 2) \times 9.8 \times 0.5 = 3 \times 4.9 = 14.7\text{ N m}$

The total moment of inertia $I$ of the system about the pivot, assuming the rod is light (massless), is the sum of the moments of inertia of the two point masses:

$I = m_1 r^2 + m_2 r^2 = (m_1 + m_2) r^2$

$I = (5 + 2) \times (0.5)^2 = 7 \times 0.25 = 1.75\text{ kg m}^2$

Using Newton's second law for rotation, $\tau = I \alpha$, we can find the initial angular acceleration $\alpha$:

$\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I} = \dfrac{14.7}{1.75} = 8.4\text{ rad/s}^2$

questions.q: As depicted in the figure, two blocks of masses $m$ and $M$ are linked by a string that passes over a pulley. The horizontal table on which the mass $m$ slides is smooth. The pulley, which can freely rotate about its axis, has a radius $r$ and a moment of inertia $I$ about this axis. Determine the acceleration of the mass $M$, assuming the string does not slip on the pulley.
questions.solution:
Let $a$ be the acceleration of the blocks and $\alpha$ be the angular acceleration of the pulley.

Since the string does not slip on the pulley, the relation between linear and angular acceleration is $a = \alpha r$.

Let $T_1$ be the tension in the horizontal segment of the string attached to mass $m$, and $T_2$ be the tension in the vertical segment attached to mass $M$.

Writing the equations of motion for each component:
For mass $M$ (moving downwards):
$Mg - T_2 = Ma$

For mass $m$ (moving horizontally on a smooth table):
$T_1 = ma$

For the pulley (rotating about its axis):
$(T_2 - T_1)r = I\alpha$

Substituting $\alpha = \dfrac{a}{r}$ into the torque equation:
$T_2 - T_1 = \dfrac{Ia}{r^2}$

Now, adding the equations for mass $M$, mass $m$, and the pulley:
$(Mg - T_2) + (T_2 - T_1) + T_1 = Ma + \dfrac{Ia}{r^2} + ma$

$Mg = a\left(M + m + \dfrac{I}{r^2}\right)$

Solving for $a$, we get:
$a = \dfrac{Mg}{M + m + \dfrac{I}{r^2}}$

questions.solution:
Let $a$ be the downward acceleration of the block and $T$ be the tension in the string.

For the block of mass $m$, the equation of motion is:
$mg - T = ma$

For the wheel, the tension $T$ provides the torque for its rotation. The equation of rotational motion is:
$\tau = I\alpha$
$TR = I\alpha$

Since the string does not slip, the linear acceleration $a$ is related to the angular acceleration $\alpha$ by:
$a = \alpha R \Rightarrow \alpha = \dfrac{a}{R}$

Substituting $\alpha$ in the torque equation:
$TR = I\left(\dfrac{a}{R}\right)$
$T = \dfrac{Ia}{R^2}$

Substituting the expression for $T$ into the block's equation of motion:
$mg - \dfrac{Ia}{R^2} = ma$
$mg = a\left(m + \dfrac{I}{R^2}\right)$
$a = \dfrac{mg}{m + \dfrac{I}{R^2}}$

Given values are:
$m = 2.0 \text{ kg}$
$g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$
$I = 0.20 \text{ kg-m}^2$
$R = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$

Calculating the equivalent mass of the wheel:
$\dfrac{I}{R^2} = \dfrac{0.20}{(0.1)^2} = \dfrac{0.20}{0.01} = 20 \text{ kg}$

Now, substituting the values to find $a$:
$a = \dfrac{2.0 \times 9.8}{2.0 + 20}$
$a = \dfrac{19.6}{22}$
$a \approx 0.89 \text{ m/s}^2$

questions.solution:
Let $a$ be the downward acceleration of block $M$. Since the string is inextensible, block $m$ will have an upward acceleration $a$.

Let $T_1$ be the tension in the string attached to $M$, $T_2$ be the tension in the horizontal segment of the string between the two pulleys, and $T_3$ be the tension in the string attached to $m$.

Writing the equations of motion for the two blocks:
For block $M$:
$Mg - T_1 = Ma$ ... (i)

For block $m$:
$T_3 - mg = ma$ ... (ii)

For the two pulleys, assuming no slipping, the angular acceleration is $\alpha = \dfrac{a}{R}$.
Writing the torque equations for the two identical pulleys:
For the first pulley (above $M$):
$(T_1 - T_2)R = I\alpha = I\left(\dfrac{a}{R}\right)$
$\Rightarrow T_1 - T_2 = \dfrac{Ia}{R^2}$ ... (iii)

For the second pulley (above $m$):
$(T_2 - T_3)R = I\alpha = I\left(\dfrac{a}{R}\right)$
$\Rightarrow T_2 - T_3 = \dfrac{Ia}{R^2}$ ... (iv)

Adding equations (iii) and (iv), we get:
$T_1 - T_3 = \dfrac{2Ia}{R^2}$ ... (v)

From equations (i) and (ii), we can substitute the values of $T_1$ and $T_3$ into equation (v):
$(Mg - Ma) - (mg + ma) = \dfrac{2Ia}{R^2}$

$(M - m)g - (M + m)a = \dfrac{2Ia}{R^2}$

$(M - m)g = a\left(M + m + \dfrac{2I}{R^2}\right)$

$a = \dfrac{(M - m)g}{M + m + \dfrac{2I}{R^2}}$

questions.solution:
Let $a$ be the acceleration of the blocks, $T_1$ be the tension in the string attached to the $2.0 \text{ kg}$ block, and $T_2$ be the tension in the string attached to the $4.0 \text{ kg}$ block.

The equations of motion for the blocks along the incline are:
For the $4.0 \text{ kg}$ block (moving downwards):
$m_2 g \sin 45^\circ - T_2 = m_2 a$

For the $2.0 \text{ kg}$ block (moving upwards):
$T_1 - m_1 g \sin 45^\circ = m_1 a$
$T_1 - 2g \sin 45^\circ = 2a$

For the rotation of the pulley:
$(T_2 - T_1)R = I\alpha$
Since the string does not slip, $\alpha = \dfrac{a}{R}$.
$\Rightarrow T_2 - T_1 = \dfrac{I}{R^2}a$

Given $I = 0.5 \text{ kg-m}^2$ and $R = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$:
$\dfrac{I}{R^2} = \dfrac{0.5}{(0.1)^2} = \dfrac{0.5}{0.01} = 50 \text{ kg}$

Adding the three equations:
$(4g \sin 45^\circ - T_2) + (T_2 - T_1) + (T_1 - 2g \sin 45^\circ) = 4a + \dfrac{I}{R^2}a + 2a$
$4g \sin 45^\circ - 2g \sin 45^\circ = \left(6 + 50\right)a$
$2g \sin 45^\circ = 56a$
$2g \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 56a$
$\sqrt{2}g = 56a$

Taking $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$ and $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$:
$a = \dfrac{1.414 \times 10}{56} = \dfrac{14.14}{56} \approx 0.25 \text{ m/s}^2$

The acceleration of the $4.0 \text{ kg}$ block is approximately $0.25 \text{ m/s}^2$.

Answer: $0.25 \text{ m/s}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform metre stick of mass $200 \text{ g}$ is suspended from the ceiling by two vertical strings of equal lengths attached at its ends. A small object of mass $20 \text{ g}$ is positioned on the stick at a distance of $70 \text{ cm}$ from the left end. Determine the tensions in the two strings.
options: $1.14 \text{ N}$ in the left string and $1.06 \text{ N}$ in the right string
$1.06 \text{ N}$ in the left string and $1.14 \text{ N}$ in the right string
$1.12 \text{ N}$ in the left string and $1.04 \text{ N}$ in the right string
$1.04 \text{ N}$ in the left string and $1.12 \text{ N}$ in the right string
questions.solution:
Let the length of the metre stick be $L = 100 \text{ cm}$.

Mass of the stick, $M = 200 \text{ g} = 0.2 \text{ kg}$.
Weight of the stick, $W_1 = Mg = 0.2 \times 9.8 = 1.96 \text{ N}$, acting at its centre of gravity ($50 \text{ cm}$ from the left end).

Mass of the small object, $m = 20 \text{ g} = 0.02 \text{ kg}$.
Weight of the object, $W_2 = mg = 0.02 \times 9.8 = 0.196 \text{ N}$, acting at $70 \text{ cm}$ from the left end.

Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be the tensions in the left and right strings respectively.

For rotational equilibrium, taking torque about the left end:
$T_2 \times 100 = W_1 \times 50 + W_2 \times 70$
$T_2 \times 100 = (1.96 \times 50) + (0.196 \times 70)$
$T_2 \times 100 = 98 + 13.72 = 111.72$
$T_2 = 1.1172 \text{ N} \approx 1.12 \text{ N}$

For translational equilibrium, balancing the vertical forces:
$T_1 + T_2 = W_1 + W_2$
$T_1 + 1.1172 = 1.96 + 0.196 = 2.156$
$T_1 = 2.156 - 1.1172 = 1.0388 \text{ N} \approx 1.04 \text{ N}$

Therefore, the tension in the left string is $1.04 \text{ N}$ and in the right string is $1.12 \text{ N}$.

Answer: $1.04 \text{ N}$ in the left string and $1.12 \text{ N}$ in the right string

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform ladder of length $10.0 \text{ m}$ and mass $16.0 \text{ kg}$ rests against a frictionless vertical wall, forming an angle of $37^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the wall. The ground is rough. An electrician weighing $60.0 \text{ kg}$ climbs the ladder and remains at a distance of $8.00 \text{ m}$ from the lower end. Determine the normal force and the force of friction exerted by the ground on the ladder, as well as the minimum coefficient of friction required for the electrician to work safely. (Take $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Let $N_g$ be the normal force exerted by the ground, $f$ be the frictional force, and $N_w$ be the normal force exerted by the frictionless wall.

Balancing the vertical forces:

$N_g = m_l g + m_e g$

$N_g = (16.0 + 60.0) \times 9.8 = 76.0 \times 9.8 = 744.8 \text{ N} \approx 745 \text{ N}$

Balancing the horizontal forces:

$f = N_w$

Taking torque about the lower end of the ladder. The ladder makes an angle of $37^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the vertical wall, so the perpendicular distances for the weights are proportional to $\sin(37^{}^{{}^{\circ}})$ and for the normal force from the wall is proportional to $\cos(37^{}^{{}^{\circ}})$:

$N_w L \cos(37^{}^{{}^{\circ}}) = m_l g \left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right) \sin(37^{}^{{}^{\circ}}) + m_e g d \sin(37^{}^{{}^{\circ}})$

$N_w \times 10.0 \times \cos(37^{}^{{}^{\circ}}) = 16.0 \times 9.8 \times 5.0 \times \sin(37^{}^{{}^{\circ}}) + 60.0 \times 9.8 \times 8.0 \times \sin(37^{}^{{}^{\circ}})$

$N_w \times 10.0 = (784 + 4704) \tan(37^{}^{{}^{\circ}})$

$N_w \times 10.0 = 5488 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 4116$

$N_w = 411.6 \text{ N}$

Thus, the force of friction is $f = 411.6 \text{ N} \approx 412 \text{ N}$.

The minimum coefficient of friction $\mu$ required for the electrician to work safely is:

$\mu = \dfrac{f}{N_g} = \dfrac{411.6}{744.8} \approx 0.553$

A mechanic stands on the ladder at a point $8.00 \text{ m}$ from the lower end. If the coefficient of friction between the ground and ladder is $0.540$, find the maximum weight of the mechanic for which the ladder remains in equilibrium.
questions.solution: Take moments about the ground contact and use the limiting friction condition $f = \mu N$. With the wall frictionless and the mechanic at $8.00 \text{ m}$, equilibrium gives a maximum mechanic mass of $44 \text{ kg}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $6.5 \text{ m}$ long ladder rests against a vertical wall, reaching a height of $6.0 \text{ m}$. A $60 \text{ kg}$ man stands halfway up the ladder. Determine the torque of the force exerted by the man on the ladder about the upper end of the ladder.
questions.solution:
Let the length of the ladder be $L = 6.5 \text{ m}$ and the height of the wall it reaches be $h = 6.0 \text{ m}$.

The distance of the base of the ladder from the wall is given by the Pythagorean theorem:
$x = \sqrt{L^2 - h^2} = \sqrt{(6.5)^2 - (6.0)^2} = \sqrt{42.25 - 36.00} = \sqrt{6.25} = 2.5 \text{ m}$

The man stands halfway up the ladder. The horizontal distance of the man from the vertical wall (which passes through the upper end of the ladder) is:
$r_{\perp} = \dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{2.5}{2} = 1.25 \text{ m}$

The force exerted by the man on the ladder is equal to his weight, acting vertically downwards:
$F = mg = 60 \times 9.8 = 588 \text{ N}$

The torque of this force about the upper end of the ladder is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force:
$\tau = F \times r_{\perp} = 588 \times 1.25 = 735 \text{ N-m}$

Rounding to two significant figures, the torque is approximately $740 \text{ N-m}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $6.5 \text{ m}$ long ladder rests against a vertical wall, reaching a height of $6.0 \text{ m}$. A $60 \text{ kg}$ man stands halfway up the ladder. Assuming the weight of the ladder to be negligible as compared to the man and assuming the wall to be smooth, determine the force exerted by the ground on the ladder.
questions.solution:
Let the length of the ladder be $L = 6.5 \text{ m}$ and the height of the wall it reaches be $h = 6.0 \text{ m}$.

The distance of the base of the ladder from the wall is $x = \sqrt{L^2 - h^2} = \sqrt{6.5^2 - 6.0^2} = 2.5 \text{ m}$.

The forces acting on the ladder are the weight of the man $W = mg = 60 \times 9.8 = 588 \text{ N} \approx 590 \text{ N}$, the normal reaction from the ground $N_V$, the horizontal friction from the ground $N_H$, and the normal reaction from the smooth wall $N_W$.

For vertical equilibrium, the vertical force exerted by the ground is:

$N_V = W \approx 590 \text{ N}$

For horizontal equilibrium, the horizontal force exerted by the ground is equal to the normal reaction from the wall:

$N_H = N_W$

Taking torque about the base of the ladder to find $N_W$:

$N_W \times h = W \times \dfrac{x}{2}$

$N_W \times 6.0 = 588 \times \dfrac{2.5}{2}$

$N_W = \dfrac{588 \times 1.25}{6.0} = 122.5 \text{ N} \approx 120 \text{ N}$

Thus, the force exerted by the ground on the ladder is $590 \text{ N}$ vertical and $120 \text{ N}$ horizontal.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An almirah door is $6 \text{ ft}$ high and $1.5 \text{ ft}$ wide, weighing $8 \text{ kg}$. It is held up by two hinges placed $1 \text{ ft}$ from its ends. Assuming the magnitudes of the forces exerted by the hinges on the door are identical, determine this magnitude.
questions.solution:
Let the acceleration due to gravity be $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
Weight of the door, $W = mg = 8 \times 10 = 80 \text{ N}$.

Let the horizontal and vertical components of the reaction force at the upper hinge be $H_1$ and $V_1$, and at the lower hinge be $H_2$ and $V_2$.

For translational equilibrium in the horizontal and vertical directions:
$\Sigma F_x = 0 \Rightarrow H_1 + H_2 = 0 \Rightarrow H_1 = -H_2$
$\Sigma F_y = 0 \Rightarrow V_1 + V_2 = W = 80 \text{ N}$

It is given that the magnitudes of the forces exerted by both hinges are identical:
$\sqrt{H_1^2 + V_1^2} = \sqrt{H_2^2 + V_2^2}$

Since $H_1^2 = H_2^2$, we get $V_1^2 = V_2^2$.
As $V_1 + V_2 = 80 \text{ N}$, we must have $V_1 = V_2 = 40 \text{ N}$.

The hinges are placed $1 \text{ ft}$ from each end of the $6 \text{ ft}$ high door.
Distance between the hinges, $d = 6 - 1 - 1 = 4 \text{ ft}$.
The center of mass of the door is at its geometric center, so its horizontal distance from the axis of the hinges is $x = \dfrac{1.5}{2} = 0.75 \text{ ft}$.

For rotational equilibrium, taking torque about the lower hinge:
$H_1 \times d + W \times x = 0$
$H_1 \times 4 + 80 \times 0.75 = 0$
$4 H_1 = -60 \Rightarrow H_1 = -15 \text{ N}$

The magnitude of the force exerted by each hinge is:
$F = \sqrt{H_1^2 + V_1^2} = \sqrt{(-15)^2 + 40^2}$
$F = \sqrt{225 + 1600} = \sqrt{1825} \approx 42.72 \text{ N}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the magnitude is $43 \text{ N}$.

Answer: $43 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod of length $L$ rests against a smooth roller, as shown in the figure. Determine the friction coefficient between the ground and the lower end, given that the minimum angle the rod can make with the horizontal is $ heta$.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the rod be $m$ and its length be $L$.

The forces acting on the rod are:
1. Weight $mg$ acting vertically downwards at the center of mass, at a distance $\dfrac{L}{2}$ from the lower end.
2. Normal reaction $N_1$ acting vertically upwards at the lower end.
3. Frictional force $f$ acting horizontally inwards at the lower end.
4. Normal reaction $N_2$ from the smooth roller, acting perpendicular to the rod.

The distance of the point of contact of the roller from the lower end along the rod is $x = \dfrac{h}{\sin\theta}$.

Taking torque about the lower end of the rod:
$N_2 \left( \dfrac{h}{\sin\theta} \right) - mg \left( \dfrac{L}{2} \cos\theta \right) = 0$
$\Rightarrow N_2 = \dfrac{mg L \cos\theta \sin\theta}{2h}$

For horizontal equilibrium:
$f = N_2 \sin\theta$

For vertical equilibrium:
$N_1 + N_2 \cos\theta = mg$
$\Rightarrow N_1 = mg - N_2 \cos\theta$

For the minimum angle $\theta$, the rod is on the verge of slipping, so $f = \mu N_1$.
$\mu = \dfrac{f}{N_1} = \dfrac{N_2 \sin\theta}{mg - N_2 \cos\theta}$

Substituting the value of $N_2$:
$\mu = \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{mg L \cos\theta \sin\theta}{2h} \right) \sin\theta}{mg - \left( \dfrac{mg L \cos\theta \sin\theta}{2h} \right) \cos\theta}$

$\mu = \dfrac{\dfrac{L \cos\theta \sin^2\theta}{2h}}{1 - \dfrac{L \cos^2\theta \sin\theta}{2h}}$

$\mu = \dfrac{L \cos\theta \sin^2\theta}{2h - L \cos^2\theta \sin\theta}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod having a mass of $300 \text{ g}$ and a length of $50 \text{ cm}$ rotates at a uniform angular speed of $2 \text{ rad/s}$ about an axis perpendicular to the rod through one end. Calculate the angular momentum of the rod about the axis of rotation.
questions.solution:
Mass of the rod, $m = 300 \text{ g} = 0.3 \text{ kg}$

Length of the rod, $l = 50 \text{ cm} = 0.5 \text{ m}$

Angular speed, $\omega = 2 \text{ rad/s}$

The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about an axis passing through one end and perpendicular to its length is:

$I = \dfrac{ml^2}{3}$

Substituting the given values:

$I = \dfrac{0.3 \times (0.5)^2}{3} = 0.1 \times 0.25 = 0.025 \text{ kg-m}^2$

The angular momentum $L$ is given by:

$L = I\omega$

Substituting the values:

$L = 0.025 \times 2 = 0.05 \text{ kg-m}^2/\text{s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod having a mass of $300 \text{ g}$ and a length of $50 \text{ cm}$ rotates at a uniform angular speed of $2 \text{ rad/s}$ about an axis perpendicular to the rod through one end. Determine the speed of the centre of the rod.
questions.solution:
Given, length of the rod $L = 50 \text{ cm}$ and angular speed $\omega = 2 \text{ rad/s}$.

The distance of the centre of the rod from the axis of rotation passing through one end is $r = \dfrac{L}{2} = 25 \text{ cm}$.

The linear speed of the centre of the rod is given by $v = r\omega$.

Substituting the values, $v = 25 \times 2 = 50 \text{ cm/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod having a mass of $300 \text{ g}$ and a length of $50 \text{ cm}$ rotates at a uniform angular speed of $2 \text{ rad/s}$ about an axis perpendicular to the rod through one end. Compute the kinetic energy of the rod.
questions.solution:
Mass of the rod, $m = 300 \text{ g} = 0.3 \text{ kg}$

Length of the rod, $l = 50 \text{ cm} = 0.5 \text{ m}$

Angular speed, $\omega = 2 \text{ rad/s}$

The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about an axis passing through one end and perpendicular to its length is:

$I = \dfrac{m l^2}{3}$

Substituting the given values:

$I = \dfrac{0.3 \times (0.5)^2}{3} = 0.1 \times 0.25 = 0.025 \text{ kg m}^2$

The rotational kinetic energy of the rod is given by:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2$

Substituting the values of $I$ and $\omega$:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.025 \times (2)^2$

$K = 0.025 \times 2 = 0.05 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Subjected to a constant torque of $0.10 \text{ N-m}$, a uniform square plate of mass $2.0 \text{ kg}$ and edge $10 \text{ cm}$ rotates about one of its diagonals. Determine the angular momentum and the kinetic energy of the plate at the end of the fifth second after starting.
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a uniform square plate of mass $m$ and side length $a$ about its diagonal is given by:

$I = \dfrac{ma^2}{12}$

Substituting the given values, $m = 2.0 \text{ kg}$ and $a = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$:

$I = \dfrac{2.0 \times (0.1)^2}{12} = \dfrac{0.02}{12} = \dfrac{1}{600} \text{ kg-m}^2$

The angular momentum $L$ after time $t = 5 \text{ s}$ under a constant torque $\tau = 0.10 \text{ N-m}$ starting from rest is:

$L = \tau t = 0.10 \times 5 = 0.5 \text{ kg-m}^2/\text{s}$

The kinetic energy $K$ of the plate is given by:

$K = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}$

Substituting the values of $L$ and $I$:

$K = \dfrac{(0.5)^2}{2 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{600}\right)} = \dfrac{0.25}{\dfrac{1}{300}} = 0.25 \times 300 = 75 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the ratio of the earth's angular momentum about its axis due to its spinning motion to its angular momentum about the sun due to its orbital motion. The radius of the earth is $6400 \text{ km}$ and the radius of the earth's orbit around the sun is $1.5 \times 10^8 \text{ km}$.
questions.solution:
The angular momentum of the earth about its own axis due to its spinning motion is given by

$L_s = I_s \omega_s = \dfrac{2}{5} M R^2 $\$left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T_s}\right)

where $M$ is the mass of the earth, $R$ is its radius, and $T_s$ is the time period of its rotation ($1 \text{ day}$).

The angular momentum of the earth about the sun due to its orbital motion is given by

$L_o = I_o \omega_o = M r^2 \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T_o}\right)$

where $r$ is the radius of the earth's orbit and $T_o$ is the time period of its revolution ($365 \text{ days}$).

The ratio of the two angular momenta is

$\dfrac{L_s}{L_o} = \dfrac{\dfrac{2}{5} M R^2 \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T_s}\right)}{M r^2 $\$left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T_o}\right)} = $\dfrac{2}{5} \left(\dfrac{R}{r}\right)^2 \$left(\dfrac{T_o}{T_s}\right)

Substituting the given values, $R = 6400 \text{ km}$, $r = 1.5 \times 10^8 \text{ km}$, $T_o = 365 \text{ days}$, and $T_s = 1 \text{ day}$:

\dfrac{L_s}{L_o} = \dfrac{2}{5} \left(\dfrac{6400}{1.5 \times 10^8}\right)^2 \times \left(\dfrac{365}{1}\right)$

$\dfrac{L_s}{L_o} = \dfrac{2}{5} \times \left(\dfrac{6.4}{1.5} \times 10^{-5}\right)^2 \times 365$

$\dfrac{L_s}{L_o} = 146 \times \left(4.267 \times 10^{-5}\right)^2$

$\dfrac{L_s}{L_o} = 146 \times 18.2 \times 10^{-10} \approx 2.66 \times 10^{-7}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ are connected by a light rigid rod of length $r$. The system rotates at an angular speed $\omega$ about an axis passing through the centre of mass of the system and perpendicular to the rod. Determine the angular momentum of the system, where $\mu$ is the reduced mass defined as $\mu = \dfrac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$.
questions.solution:
Let the distances of the masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ from the centre of mass be $r_1$ and $r_2$ respectively.

$r_1 = \dfrac{m_2 r}{m_1 + m_2}$ and $r_2 = \dfrac{m_1 r}{m_1 + m_2}$

The moment of inertia of the system about the axis passing through the centre of mass and perpendicular to the rod is

$I = m_1 r_1^2 + m_2 r_2^2$

Substituting the values of $r_1$ and $r_2$:

$I = m_1 \left( \dfrac{m_2 r}{m_1 + m_2} \right)^2 + m_2 \left( \dfrac{m_1 r}{m_1 + m_2} \right)^2$

$I = \dfrac{m_1 m_2^2 r^2}{(m_1 + m_2)^2} + \dfrac{m_2 m_1^2 r^2}{(m_1 + m_2)^2}$

$I = \dfrac{m_1 m_2 (m_1 + m_2) r^2}{(m_1 + m_2)^2}$

$I = \dfrac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2} r^2 = \mu r^2$

The angular momentum of the system is given by $L = I \omega$

$L = \mu r^2 \omega$

questions.q: Two identical small balls, each having a mass of $1/2 \text{ kg}$, are attached to the ends of a light rod that is $50 \text{ cm}$ long to form a dumb-bell. This dumb-bell rotates at an angular speed of $10 \text{ rad/s}$ about a fixed axis passing perpendicular to the rod through its centre. For $0.10 \text{ s}$, an impulsive force with an average magnitude of $5.0 \text{ N}$ is applied to one of the masses in the direction of its velocity. Determine the new angular velocity of the system.
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of the dumb-bell system about the axis of rotation is given by:

$I = 2mr^2$

Substituting $m = 0.5 \text{ kg}$ and $r = \dfrac{0.5}{2} = 0.25 \text{ m}$:

$I = 2 \times 0.5 \times (0.25)^2 = 0.0625 \text{ kg m}^2$

The initial angular momentum of the system is:

$L_i = I\omega_0 = 0.0625 \times 10 = 0.625 \text{ kg m}^2/\text{s}$

The torque produced by the impulsive force about the centre is:

$\tau = F \times r = 5.0 \times 0.25 = 1.25 \text{ N m}$

The angular impulse applied to the system is:

$\Delta L = \tau \Delta t = 1.25 \times 0.10 = 0.125 \text{ kg m}^2/\text{s}$

Since the force is applied in the direction of velocity, the angular momentum increases. The final angular momentum is:

$L_f = L_i + \Delta L = 0.625 + 0.125 = 0.750 \text{ kg m}^2/\text{s}$

The new angular velocity is:

$\omega_f = \dfrac{L_f}{I} = \dfrac{0.750}{0.0625} = 12 \text{ rad/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wheel having a moment of inertia of $0.500 \text{ kg-m}^2$ and a radius of $20.0 \text{ cm}$ is rotating about its axis with an angular speed of $20.0 \text{ rad/s}$. It picks up a stationary particle of mass $200 \text{ g}$ at its edge. Determine the new angular speed of the wheel.
questions.solution:
Initial moment of inertia of the wheel, $I_1 = 0.500 \text{ kg-m}^2$

Initial angular speed, $\omega_1 = 20.0 \text{ rad/s}$

Mass of the particle, $m = 200 \text{ g} = 0.200 \text{ kg}$

Radius of the wheel, $r = 20.0 \text{ cm} = 0.200 \text{ m}$

Moment of inertia of the particle about the axis of rotation, $I_p = m r^2 = 0.200 \times (0.200)^2 = 0.008 \text{ kg-m}^2$

Final moment of inertia of the system, $I_2 = I_1 + I_p = 0.500 + 0.008 = 0.508 \text{ kg-m}^2$

By the principle of conservation of angular momentum:

$I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2$

$0.500 \times 20.0 = 0.508 \times \omega_2$

$\omega_2 = \dfrac{10.0}{0.508} \approx 19.7 \text{ rad/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A diver with a moment of inertia of $6.0 \text{ kg-m}^2$ about an axis passing through his centre of mass rotates about this axis at an angular speed of $2 \text{ rad/s}$. If the diver folds his hands and feet, reducing the moment of inertia to $5.0 \text{ kg-m}^2$, what will be the new angular speed?
questions.solution:
According to the principle of conservation of angular momentum, if no external torque acts on a system, its total angular momentum remains constant.

Initial angular momentum $L_1 = I_1 \omega_1$

Final angular momentum $L_2 = I_2 \omega_2$

Equating the initial and final angular momentum:

$I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2$

Substituting the given values:

$6.0 \times 2 = 5.0 \times \omega_2$

$\omega_2 = \dfrac{12.0}{5.0} = 2.4 \text{ rad/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A boy sits in a revolving chair that rotates at an angular speed of $120$ revolutions per minute. Two heavy balls are part of the revolving system, and the boy can pull the balls closer to himself or push them apart. If the boy decreases the moment of inertia of the system from $6 \text{ kg-m}^2$ to $2 \text{ kg-m}^2$ by pulling the balls closer, determine the new angular speed.
questions.solution:
According to the principle of conservation of angular momentum, if no external torque acts on a system, its total angular momentum remains constant.

$I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2$

Given:
$I_1 = 6 \text{ kg-m}^2$
$\omega_1 = 120 \text{ rpm}$
$I_2 = 2 \text{ kg-m}^2$

Substituting the values into the equation:

$6 \times 120 = 2 \times \omega_2$

$\omega_2 = \dfrac{6 \times 120}{2}$

$\omega_2 = 360 \text{ rpm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wheel with a moment of inertia of $0.10 \text{ kg-m}^2$ rotates about a shaft at an angular speed of $160 \text{ rev/minute}$. A second wheel is set into rotation at $300 \text{ rev/minute}$ and is then coupled to the same shaft, causing both wheels to finally rotate at a common angular speed of $200 \text{ rev/minute}$. Determine the moment of inertia of the second wheel.
questions.solution:
By conservation of angular momentum:

$I_1 \omega_1 + I_2 \omega_2 = (I_1 + I_2) \omega$

Given $I_1 = 0.10 \text{ kg-m}^2$, $\omega_1 = 160 \text{ rev/minute}$, $\omega_2 = 300 \text{ rev/minute}$, and $\omega = 200 \text{ rev/minute}$.

Substituting the values:

$0.10 \times 160 + I_2 \times 300 = (0.10 + I_2) \times 200$

$16 + 300 I_2 = 20 + 200 I_2$

$100 I_2 = 4$

$I_2 = 0.04 \text{ kg-m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A boy stands on a platform that can freely rotate about its vertical axis. He is holding an open umbrella, with the umbrella's axis coinciding with that of the platform. The moment of inertia for the "platform plus boy" system is $3.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg-m}^2$, and for the umbrella it is $2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg-m}^2$. The boy then begins to spin the umbrella about the axis at an angular speed of $2.0 \text{ rev/s}$ relative to himself. Calculate the angular velocity imparted to the platform.
questions.solution:
Let $I_1$ be the moment of inertia of the platform plus boy, and $I_2$ be the moment of inertia of the umbrella.

$I_1 = 3.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg-m}^2$

$I_2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg-m}^2$

Let $\omega_1$ be the angular velocity of the platform relative to the ground. The angular velocity of the umbrella relative to the platform is $\omega_{rel} = 2.0 \text{ rev/s}$.

The angular velocity of the umbrella relative to the ground is $\omega_2 = \omega_1 + \omega_{rel}$.

Since no external torque acts on the system about the vertical axis, the total angular momentum is conserved.

$L_i = L_f$

$0 = I_1 \omega_1 + I_2 \omega_2$

$0 = I_1 \omega_1 + I_2 (\omega_1 + \omega_{rel})$

$(I_1 + I_2) \omega_1 = -I_2 \omega_{rel}$

$\omega_1 = -\dfrac{I_2 \omega_{rel}}{I_1 + I_2}$

Substituting the given values:

$\omega_1 = -\dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 2.0}{3.0 \times 10^{-3} + 2.0 \times 10^{-3}}$

$\omega_1 = -\dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-3}}{5.0 \times 10^{-3}}$

$\omega_1 = -0.8 \text{ rev/s}$

The negative sign indicates that the platform rotates in the direction opposite to the umbrella's rotation. The magnitude of the angular velocity imparted to the platform is $0.8 \text{ rev/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A kid of mass $M$ stands at the edge of a platform of radius $R$ which can rotate freely about its axis. The moment of inertia of the platform is $I$. The system is initially at rest, and the kid holds a ball of mass $m$ while standing on the rim. He throws the ball horizontally, tangential to the rim, with speed $v$ as seen by his friend. Find the angular velocity with which the platform starts rotating.
questions.solution: $\dfrac{mvR}{I + MR^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A kid of mass $M$ stands at the edge of a platform of radius $R$, which is free to rotate about its axis. The moment of inertia of the platform is $I$. The system is initially at rest when a friend tosses a ball of mass $m$, and the kid catches it. If the ball's velocity is $v$ horizontally along the tangent to the platform's edge at the moment it is caught, determine the angular speed of the platform following the event.
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of angular momentum about the axis of rotation of the platform, the initial angular momentum of the system is equal to the final angular momentum.

The initial angular momentum of the system is entirely due to the ball, as the platform and the kid are initially at rest. Since the ball is moving horizontally along the tangent to the edge of the platform of radius $R$, its angular momentum is:

$L_i = mvR$

After the kid catches the ball, the platform, the kid, and the ball rotate together with an angular speed $\omega$. The total moment of inertia of the system about the axis of rotation is the sum of the moments of inertia of the platform, the kid, and the ball. Both the kid and the ball are at a distance $R$ from the axis.

$I_{total} = I + MR^2 + mR^2 = I + (M + m)R^2$

The final angular momentum of the system is:

$L_f = I_{total}\omega = [I + (M + m)R^2]\omega$

Equating the initial and final angular momentum:

$mvR = [I + (M + m)R^2]\omega$

$\omega = \dfrac{mvR}{I + (M + m)R^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A kid of mass $M$ stands at the edge of a platform of radius $R$ which can rotate freely about its axis. The moment of inertia of the platform is $I$. The system is rotating anticlockwise with angular speed $\omega$ while the kid stands on the rim. The kid then walks along the rim in the anticlockwise direction with speed $v$ relative to the platform. Find the new angular speed of the platform.
questions.solution: $\omega - \dfrac{MvR}{I + MR^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod of mass $m$ and length $l$ is struck at one end by a force $F$ perpendicular to the rod for a short duration $t$. Assuming $t$ is small enough that the rod does not appreciably alter its direction while the force acts, determine the speed of the centre of mass after the force has stopped acting.
questions.solution:
The impulse delivered to the rod is given by the product of the force and the time duration:

$J = Ft$

According to the impulse-momentum theorem, the net linear impulse applied to a system is equal to the change in its linear momentum. The point of application of the force affects the angular velocity but does not affect the linear velocity of the centre of mass.

$J = \Delta p_{cm}$

$Ft = m v_{cm} - 0$

$v_{cm} = \dfrac{Ft}{m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod of mass $m$ and length $l$ is struck at one end by a force $F$ perpendicular to the rod for a brief time interval $t$. Assuming that $t$ is so small that the rod does not noticeably alter its direction while the force acts, calculate the angular speed of the rod about its centre of mass after the force ceases to act.
questions.solution:
The angular impulse about the centre of mass is given by the product of torque and time.

Torque $\tau = F \times \dfrac{l}{2}$

Angular impulse $= \dfrac{F l t}{2}$

Change in angular momentum $\Delta L = I \omega$

The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about an axis passing through its centre of mass and perpendicular to its length is $I = \dfrac{m l^2}{12}$

Equating the angular impulse to the change in angular momentum:

$\dfrac{m l^2}{12} \omega = \dfrac{F l t}{2}$

$\omega = \dfrac{12 F l t}{2 m l^2}$

$\omega = \dfrac{6 F t}{m l}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod of mass $m$ and length $l$ is struck at one end by a force $F$ perpendicular to the rod for a short time interval $t$. Assuming $t$ is so brief that the rod does not appreciably change its orientation while the force is applied, compute the kinetic energy of the rod after the force has stopped acting.
questions.solution:
The linear impulse applied to the rod is $J = F t$.

This impulse provides a translational velocity to the center of mass, given by $v = \dfrac{J}{m} = \dfrac{F t}{m}$.

The angular impulse about the center of mass is the product of the linear impulse and the perpendicular distance from the center of mass, which is $L = J \times \dfrac{l}{2} = \dfrac{F t l}{2}$.

The moment of inertia of the uniform rod about its center of mass is $I = \dfrac{m l^2}{12}$.

The translational kinetic energy is $K_{trans} = \dfrac{p^2}{2m} = \dfrac{(F t)^2}{2m} = \dfrac{F^2 t^2}{2m}$.

The rotational kinetic energy is $K_{rot} = \dfrac{L^2}{2I} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{F t l}{2}\right)^2}{2 \left(\dfrac{m l^2}{12}\right)} = \dfrac{\dfrac{F^2 t^2 l^2}{4}}{\dfrac{m l^2}{6}} = \dfrac{3 F^2 t^2}{2m}$.

The total kinetic energy of the rod after the force has stopped acting is the sum of the translational and rotational kinetic energies:

$K = K_{trans} + K_{rot} = \dfrac{F^2 t^2}{2m} + \dfrac{3 F^2 t^2}{2m} = \dfrac{4 F^2 t^2}{2m} = \dfrac{2 F^2 t^2}{m}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod of mass $m$ and length $l$ is struck at one end by a force $F$ perpendicular to the rod for a short duration $t$. Assuming that $t$ is so small that the rod does not appreciably change its direction while the force acts, find the angular momentum of the rod about its centre of mass after the force ceases to act.
questions.solution:
The angular impulse provided by the force about the centre of mass is equal to the change in angular momentum of the rod about its centre of mass.

The torque acting on the rod about its centre of mass is $\tau = F \times \dfrac{l}{2}$.

The angular impulse is given by $J = \tau t = F \left(\dfrac{l}{2}\right) t = \dfrac{Flt}{2}$.

Since the initial angular momentum is zero, the final angular momentum $L$ is equal to the angular impulse.

Thus, $L = \dfrac{Flt}{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod of length $L$ rests on a smooth horizontal table. A particle moving on the table perpendicularly strikes the rod at one end and stops. Determine the distance travelled by the centre of the rod by the time it turns through a right angle. (Note that if the mass of the rod is four times that of the particle, the collision is elastic.)
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the particle be $m$ and its initial velocity be $v$. Let the mass of the rod be $M$.

Since the particle stops after the collision, by conservation of linear momentum, the velocity of the centre of mass of the rod $v_c$ is given by:

$mv = Mv_c \Rightarrow v_c = \dfrac{mv}{M}$

By conservation of angular momentum about the centre of the rod:

$mv\dfrac{L}{2} = I\omega$

Substituting the moment of inertia of the rod $I = \dfrac{ML^2}{12}$:

$mv\dfrac{L}{2} = \dfrac{ML^2}{12}\omega \Rightarrow \omega = \dfrac{6mv}{ML}$

The time $t$ taken by the rod to turn through a right angle \left(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ is:

$t = \dfrac{\theta}{\omega} = \dfrac{\pi/2}{\dfrac{6mv}{ML}} = \dfrac{\pi ML}{12mv}$

The distance $d$ travelled by the centre of the rod during this time is:

$d = v_c t = \left(\dfrac{mv}{M}\right)\left(\dfrac{\pi ML}{12mv}\right) = \dfrac{\pi L}{12}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod of length $L$ and mass $M$ lies on a smooth horizontal table. A particle of mass $m$ moving on the table strikes the rod perpendicularly at one end with speed $v$ and sticks to it. (a) Find the velocity of the centre of mass $C$ of the system "rod + particle". (b) Find the velocity of the particle with respect to $C$ before the collision. (c) Find the velocity of the rod with respect to $C$ before the collision. (d) Find the angular momentum of the particle and of the rod about $C$ before the collision. (e) Find the moment of inertia of the system about the vertical axis through $C$ after the collision. (f) Find the velocity of $C$ and the angular velocity of the system about $C$ after the collision.
options: (a) $\dfrac{mv}{M + m}$ (b) $\dfrac{Mv}{M + m}$ (c) $-\dfrac{mv}{M + m}$ (d) $\dfrac{M^2 m v L}{2(M + m)^2}$, $\dfrac{M m^2 v L}{2(M + m)^2}$ (e) $\dfrac{M(M + 4m)L^2}{12(M + m)}$ (f) $\dfrac{mv}{M + m}$, $\dfrac{6mv}{(M + 4m)L}$

(a) $\dfrac{mv}{M + m}$ (b) $\dfrac{Mv}{M + m}$ (c) $-\dfrac{mv}{M + m}$ (d) $\dfrac{M^2 m v L}{(M + m)^2}$, $\dfrac{M m^2 v L}{(M + m)^2}$ (e) $\dfrac{M(M + 2m)L^2}{12(M + m)}$ (f) $\dfrac{mv}{M + m}$, $\dfrac{3mv}{(M + 2m)L}$

(a) $\dfrac{mv}{M + m}$ (b) $\dfrac{mv}{M + m}$ (c) $-\dfrac{Mv}{M + m}$ (d) $\dfrac{M m v L}{(M + m)^2}$, $\dfrac{M m v L}{(M + m)^2}$ (e) $\dfrac{(M + m)L^2}{12}$ (f) $\dfrac{mv}{M + m}$, $\dfrac{6mv}{(M + m)L}$
questions.solution:
(a) $\dfrac{mv}{M + m}$
(b) $\dfrac{Mv}{M + m}$
(c) $-\dfrac{mv}{M + m}$
(d) $\dfrac{M^2 mvl}{2(M + m)^2}$, $\dfrac{Mm^2 vl}{2(M + m)^2}$
(e) $\dfrac{M(M + 4m)L^2}{12(M + m)}$
(f) $\dfrac{mv}{M + m}$, $\dfrac{6mv}{(M + 4m)L}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two small balls $A$ and $B$, each having mass $m$, are rigidly connected by a light horizontal rod of length $L$. The rod is clamped at its centre such that it can freely rotate about a vertical axis passing through the centre. The system is set into rotation with an angular speed $\omega$ about this axis. A stationary particle $P$ of mass $m$ sticks to ball $A$ upon collision. Determine the new angular speed of the rod.
questions.solution:
The initial moment of inertia of the system about the vertical axis of rotation is

$I_i = m\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)^2 + m\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{mL^2}{2}$

The initial angular momentum of the system is

$L_i = I_i \omega = \dfrac{mL^2}{2} \omega$

When the stationary particle of mass $m$ sticks to ball $A$, the mass at $A$ becomes $2m$. The final moment of inertia of the system is

$I_f = 2m\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)^2 + m\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{3mL^2}{4}$

Since no external torque acts on the system about the axis of rotation, the angular momentum is conserved. Equating the initial and final angular momentum:

$L_i = L_f$

$\dfrac{mL^2}{2} \omega = \dfrac{3mL^2}{4} \omega'$

$\omega' = \dfrac{2\omega}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two small balls $A$ and $B$, each having mass $m$, are rigidly attached to the ends of a light rod of length $L$ as depicted in the figure. On a frictionless horizontal surface, the system translates with a velocity $v_0$ in a direction perpendicular to the rod. A particle $P$ of mass $m$, initially at rest on the surface, sticks to the ball $A$ when they collide. Determine the linear speeds of the balls $A$ and $B$ immediately after the collision. [Hint: The light rod will exert a force on the ball $B$ only along its length.]
questions.solution:
According to the given hint, the light rod can exert an impulsive force only along its length.

During the collision, the impulsive force between particle $P$ and ball $A$ acts in a direction perpendicular to the rod. Since the rod cannot transmit any impulse perpendicular to its length, it exerts zero transverse impulse on ball $B$.

As a result, the velocity of ball $B$ remains unchanged immediately after the collision:

$v_B = v_0$

For the system comprising ball $A$ and particle $P$, there is no external impulsive force in the direction perpendicular to the rod. Applying the principle of conservation of linear momentum for this system in the transverse direction:

$m v_0 + m(0) = (m + m) v_A$

$m v_0 = 2m v_A \Rightarrow v_A = \dfrac{v_0}{2}$

The impulse along the rod must be zero because the relative velocity of $A$ and $B$ along the rod must remain zero, and there are no initial velocities or external impulses in that direction. Thus, the linear speeds immediately after the collision are $\dfrac{v_0}{2}$ and $v_0$.

On a frictionless horizontal surface, the system translates with a velocity $v_0$ in a direction perpendicular to the rod. questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two small balls $A$ and $B$, each having mass $m$, are rigidly connected to the ends of a light rod of length $L$. The system translates on a frictionless horizontal surface with a velocity $v_0$ in a direction perpendicular to the rod. A particle $P$ of mass $m$, initially at rest on the surface, sticks to the ball $A$ upon collision. Calculate the velocity of the centre of mass $C$ of the system $A + B + P$ subsequent to the collision.
options: $\dfrac{1}{2}v_0$ along the initial motion of the rod
$\dfrac{2}{3}v_0$ along the initial motion of the rod
$v_0$ along the initial motion of the rod
$\dfrac{1}{3}v_0$ along the initial motion of the rod
questions.solution:
Let the initial direction of motion of the rod be along the positive x-axis.

The system consists of three masses: ball $A$, ball $B$, and particle $P$.
Mass of ball $A$, $m_A = m$
Mass of ball $B$, $m_B = m$
Mass of particle $P$, $m_P = m$

Initial velocities of the components are:
$\vec{v}_A = v_0 \hat{i}$
$\vec{v}_B = v_0 \hat{i}$
$\vec{v}_P = 0$

The total initial linear momentum of the system $A + B + P$ is:
$\vec{P}_i = m_A \vec{v}_A + m_B \vec{v}_B + m_P \vec{v}_P$
$\vec{P}_i = m(v_0 \hat{i}) + m(v_0 \hat{i}) + m(0) = 2mv_0 \hat{i}$

Since there are no external horizontal forces acting on the system, the total linear momentum is conserved during the collision.
Let $\vec{v}_{cm}$ be the velocity of the centre of mass of the system after the collision. The total mass of the system is $M = m_A + m_B + m_P = 3m$.

The final linear momentum of the system is:
$\vec{P}_f = M \vec{v}_{cm} = 3m \vec{v}_{cm}$

By conservation of linear momentum:
$\vec{P}_i = \vec{P}_f$
$2mv_0 \hat{i} = 3m \vec{v}_{cm}$
$\vec{v}_{cm} = \dfrac{2}{3}v_0 \hat{i}$

Thus, the velocity of the centre of mass of the system is $\dfrac{2}{3}v_0$ along the initial motion of the rod.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two small balls $A$ and $B$, each with mass $m$, are rigidly attached to the ends of a light rod of length $L$. Over a frictionless horizontal surface, the system translates with a velocity $v_0$ directed perpendicular to the rod. A stationary particle $P$ of mass $m$ on the surface sticks to ball $A$ as the ball collides with it. Compute the angular speed of the system about its centre of mass $C$ following the collision.
questions.solution:
Let the new centre of mass of the system after the collision be $C'$.
After the stationary particle $P$ sticks to ball $A$, the mass at $A$ becomes $m + m = 2m$, while the mass at $B$ remains $m$.
The distance of the new centre of mass $C'$ from $A$ is:

$x = \dfrac{m \times L + 2m \times 0}{3m} = \dfrac{L}{3}$

The distance of $C'$ from $B$ is $L - \dfrac{L}{3} = \dfrac{2L}{3}$.

The moment of inertia of the system about $C'$ after the collision is:

$I = 2m\left(\dfrac{L}{3}\right)^2 + m\left(\dfrac{2L}{3}\right)^2$

$I = \dfrac{2mL^2}{9} + \dfrac{4mL^2}{9} = \dfrac{2mL^2}{3}$

We apply the principle of conservation of angular momentum about $C'$ just before and after the collision. Before the collision, the angular momentum of the system about $C'$ is the sum of the angular momenta of balls $A$ and $B$ (since particle $P$ is stationary). Taking the direction of rotation into account:

$L_i = m v_0 \left(\dfrac{L}{3}\right) - m v_0 \left(\dfrac{2L}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{mv_0L}{3}$

The magnitude of the initial angular momentum is $L_i = \dfrac{mv_0L}{3}$.

After the collision, the system rotates about $C'$ with angular speed $\omega$. The final angular momentum is:

$L_f = I\omega = \left(\dfrac{2mL^2}{3}\right)\omega$

Equating the magnitudes of initial and final angular momentum ($L_i = L_f$):

$\dfrac{2mL^2}{3}\omega = \dfrac{mv_0L}{3}$

$\omega = \dfrac{v_0}{2L}$

Answer: $\dfrac{v_0}{2L}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two small balls $A$ and $B$, each of mass $m$, are joined rigidly to the ends of a light rod of length $L$ as shown. The rod is clamped at its centre so that it can rotate freely about a horizontal axis through the clamp. The system is held at rest in the horizontal position. A particle $P$ of mass $m$ is dropped from a height $h$ onto the ball $B$ and sticks to it. (a) Find the angular momentum and the angular speed of the system just after the collision. (b) Find the minimum value of $h$ so that the system makes a full rotation after the collision.
questions.solution:
(a) $\dfrac{mL\sqrt{gh}}{\sqrt{2}}$, $\sqrt{\dfrac{8gh}{3L}}$
(b) $\dfrac{3L}{2}$

The rod is clamped at its centre so that it can rotate freely about a horizontal axis through the clamp. The system is held at rest in the horizontal position. A particle $P$ of mass $m$ is dropped from a height $h$ onto the ball $B$ and sticks to it. (a) Find the angular momentum and the angular speed of the system just after the collision. questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two blocks having masses of $400 \text{ g}$ and $200 \text{ g}$ are connected by a light string passing over a pulley that is free to rotate about its axis. The pulley possesses a moment of inertia of $1.6 \times 10^{-4} \text{ kg-m}^2$ and a radius of $2.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the kinetic energy of the system when the $400 \text{ g}$ block falls through a distance of $50 \text{ cm}$.
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the gain in the total kinetic energy of the system is equal to the net loss in its potential energy.

Let $m_1 = 400 \text{ g} = 0.4 \text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 200 \text{ g} = 0.2 \text{ kg}$.

When the heavier block $m_1$ falls through a distance $h = 50 \text{ cm} = 0.5 \text{ m}$, the lighter block $m_2$ rises by the same distance $h$.

The net loss in potential energy of the system is given by:

$\Delta U = m_1 g h - m_2 g h = (m_1 - m_2) g h$

Substituting the given values and taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$\Delta U = (0.4 - 0.2) \times 9.8 \times 0.5$

$\Delta U = 0.2 \times 9.8 \times 0.5 = 0.98 \text{ J}$

Since the system starts from rest, the total kinetic energy of the system (including the translational kinetic energy of both blocks and the rotational kinetic energy of the pulley) is equal to the net loss in potential energy.

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the system is $0.98 \text{ J}$.

questions.q: Two blocks having masses of $400 \text{ g}$ and $200 \text{ g}$ are connected by a light string passing over a pulley that is free to rotate about its axis. The pulley possesses a moment of inertia of $1.6 \times 10^{-4} \text{ kg-m}^2$ and a radius of $2.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the speed of the blocks when the $400 \text{ g}$ block falls through a distance of $50 \text{ cm}$.
questions.solution:
Using the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the loss in potential energy of the system is equal to the gain in kinetic energy of the system.

$(m_1 - m_2)gh = \dfrac{1}{2}m_1v^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}m_2v^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

Since the string does not slip over the pulley, $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$. Substituting this into the equation gives:

$(m_1 - m_2)gh = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(m_1 + m_2 + \dfrac{I}{R^2}\right) v^2$

Given values are $m_1 = 0.4 \text{ kg}$, $m_2 = 0.2 \text{ kg}$, $h = 0.5 \text{ m}$, $R = 0.02 \text{ m}$, $I = 1.6 \times 10^{-4} \text{ kg-m}^2$, and taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$(0.4 - 0.2) \times 9.8 \times 0.5 = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(0.4 + 0.2 + \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-4}}{(0.02)^2}\right) v^2$

$0.2 \times 4.9 = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(0.6 + \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-4}}{4 \times 10^{-4}}\right) v^2$

$0.98 = \dfrac{1}{2} (0.6 + 0.4) v^2$

$0.98 = \dfrac{1}{2} (1.0) v^2$

$v^2 = 1.96 \Rightarrow v = 1.4 \text{ m/s}$
