questions.q: As illustrated in the figure, a pulley possesses a radius of $20 \text{ cm}$ and a moment of inertia of $0.2 \text{ kg-m}^2$. A string passing over it connects to a vertical spring (spring constant $50 \text{ N/m}$) fixed from below at one end, and holds a $1 \text{ kg}$ mass at the other. With the spring initially at its natural length, the system is released from rest. Determine the speed of the block once it has descended through $10 \text{ cm}$. Assume $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the loss in gravitational potential energy of the block is equal to the gain in kinetic energy of the block and the pulley, plus the gain in elastic potential energy of the spring.

Let $v$ be the speed of the block and $\omega$ be the angular speed of the pulley after the block has descended by a distance $h$. Since the string does not slip, we have $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$.

The energy conservation equation is:
$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}kh^2$

Substituting $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$:
$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\left(\dfrac{v}{R}\right)^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}kh^2$

$mgh - \dfrac{1}{2}kh^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(m + \dfrac{I}{R^2}\right)v^2$

Given values:
$m = 1 \text{ kg}$
$g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$
$h = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$
$k = 50 \text{ N/m}$
$I = 0.2 \text{ kg-m}^2$
$R = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$

Now, substituting the given values into the equation:
$1 \times 10 \times 0.1 - \dfrac{1}{2} \times 50 \times (0.1)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 + \dfrac{0.2}{(0.2)^2}\right)v^2$

$1 - 25 \times 0.01 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 + \dfrac{0.2}{0.04}\right)v^2$

$1 - 0.25 = \dfrac{1}{2}(1 + 5)v^2$

$0.75 = \dfrac{1}{2}(6)v^2$

$0.75 = 3v^2$

$v^2 = \dfrac{0.75}{3} = 0.25$

$v = \sqrt{0.25} = 0.5 \text{ m/s}$

questions.q: A metre stick is positioned vertically with one end resting on a rough horizontal floor. It is gently released to fall onto the floor. Assuming the end on the floor does not slip, determine the angular speed of the rod just as it strikes the floor. (Take $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Using conservation of mechanical energy:

Loss in potential energy = Gain in rotational kinetic energy

$mg\dfrac{L}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

Since the rod rotates about its lower end, its moment of inertia is $I = \dfrac{mL^2}{3}$.

$mg\dfrac{L}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{mL^2}{3}\right)\omega^2$

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{3g}{L}$

Given $L = 1 \text{ m}$ and $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 \times 9.8}{1}} = \sqrt{29.4} \approx 5.4 \text{ rad/s}$

questions.q: Pivoted at its upper end, a metre stick weighing $240 \text{ g}$ is able to freely rotate in a vertical plane through this end, as shown in the figure. A particle of mass $100 \text{ g}$ is attached to the upper end of the stick by a light string of length $1 \text{ m}$. Initially, the rod is held vertical and the string horizontal when the system is released from rest. The particle collides with the stick's lower end and sticks to it. Determine the maximum angle through which the stick will rise.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the stick be $M = 240 \text{ g}$ and its length be $L = 1 \text{ m}$.
Let the mass of the particle be $m = 100 \text{ g}$.

The particle falls through a height $L$, so its velocity just before the collision is $v = \sqrt{2gL}$.
The angular momentum of the particle about the pivot just before the collision is:
$L_i = m v L = m L \sqrt{2gL}$

After the collision, the particle sticks to the lower end of the stick. The moment of inertia of the system (stick + particle) about the pivot is:
$I = I_{\text{stick}} + I_{\text{particle}} = \dfrac{M L^2}{3} + m L^2 = \left(\dfrac{M}{3} + m\right) L^2$

By conservation of angular momentum about the pivot during the collision:
$L_i = I \omega \Rightarrow \omega = \dfrac{m L \sqrt{2gL}}{\left(\dfrac{M}{3} + m\right) L^2}$

The kinetic energy of the system just after the collision is:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2 = \dfrac{L_i^2}{2I} = \dfrac{m^2 L^2 (2gL)}{2 \left(\dfrac{M}{3} + m\right) L^2} = \dfrac{m^2 g L}{\dfrac{M}{3} + m}$

When the system swings to a maximum angle $\theta$, the center of mass of the stick rises by $\dfrac{L}{2}(1 - \cos\theta)$ and the particle rises by $L(1 - \cos\theta)$. The increase in potential energy is:
$U = M g \dfrac{L}{2} (1 - \cos\theta) + m g L (1 - \cos\theta) = \left(\dfrac{M}{2} + m\right) g L (1 - \cos\theta)$

By conservation of mechanical energy after the collision, $K = U$:
$\dfrac{m^2 g L}{\dfrac{M}{3} + m} = \left(\dfrac{M}{2} + m\right) g L (1 - \cos\theta)$

Substituting $M = 240 \text{ g}$ and $m = 100 \text{ g}$:
$\dfrac{100^2}{\dfrac{240}{3} + 100} = \left(\dfrac{240}{2} + 100\right) (1 - \cos\theta)$

$\dfrac{10000}{80 + 100} = (120 + 100) (1 - \cos\theta)$

$\dfrac{10000}{180} = 220 (1 - \cos\theta)$

$1 - \cos\theta = \dfrac{10000}{180 \times 220} = \dfrac{100}{396} = \dfrac{25}{99}$

$\cos\theta = 1 - \dfrac{25}{99} = \dfrac{74}{99} \approx 0.747$

Since $\cos 41^\circ \approx 0.754$ and $\cos 42^\circ \approx 0.743$, the angle $\theta$ is approximately $41^\circ$.

Answer: $\approx 41^\circ$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod, pivoted at its upper end, hangs vertically. It is displaced by an angle of $60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ and subsequently released. Determine the magnitude of the force acting on a particle of mass $dm$ located at the tip of the rod when it forms an angle of $37^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the vertical.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the uniform rod be $M$ and its length be $L$. The moment of inertia of the rod about the pivot is $I = \dfrac{ML^2}{3}$.

When the rod is at an angle $\theta = 37^\circ$ with the vertical, the torque about the pivot is provided by the weight of the rod acting at its center of mass:

$\tau = Mg \dfrac{L}{2} \sin 37^\circ$

Using $\tau = I\alpha$, the angular acceleration $\alpha$ is:

$\dfrac{ML^2}{3} \alpha = Mg \dfrac{L}{2} $\$left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)

$\alpha = $\dfrac{3g}{2L} \times \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{9g}{10L} = \dfrac{0.9g}{L}

The tangential acceleration of the particle at the tip of the rod is:

$a_t = \alpha L = 0.9g$

To find the angular velocity $\omega$ at $\theta = 37^\circ$, we use the conservation of mechanical energy. The rod is released from rest at $\theta_0 = 60^\circ$. The decrease in potential energy is equal to the gain in kinetic energy:

$\Delta U = Mg $\dfrac{L}{2} (\cos$37^\circ - \cos 60^\circ) = $\dfrac{1}{2}$I \omega^2$

$Mg $\dfrac{L}{2} \left( \dfrac{4}{5} - \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{ML^2}{3} \right) \omega^2$

$Mg $\dfrac{L}{2} \left( \dfrac{3}{10} \right) = \dfrac{ML^2}{6} \omega^2$

\dfrac{3g}{20} = \dfrac{L}{6} \omega^2 \Rightarrow \omega^2 = $\dfrac{18g}{20L} = \dfrac{0.9g}{L}

The radial (centripetal) acceleration of the particle at the tip is:

$a_r = \omega^2 L = 0.9g$

The net acceleration of the particle of mass $dm$ is the vector sum of its tangential and radial accelerations:

$a = $\sqrt{a_t^2 + a_r^2} = \sqrt{(0.9g)^2 + (0.9g)^2} =$0.$9\sqrt{2}$g$

According to Newton's second law, the magnitude of the net force acting on the particle is:

$F = dm \times a = 0.$9\sqrt{2}$\,dm\,g$

Answer: $0.$9\sqrt{2}$\,dm\,g

questions.q: A cylinder is rolling on a horizontal plane surface. Given that the speed of its centre is $25 \text{ m/s}$, determine the speed of its highest point.
questions.solution:
For a cylinder rolling on a horizontal surface, the condition for pure rolling is $v_{cm} = \omega R$.

The velocity of the highest point is the vector sum of the translational velocity of the centre of mass and the tangential velocity due to rotation.

At the highest point, both velocities are in the same direction.

$v_{top} = v_{cm} + \omega R = 2v_{cm}$

Given $v_{cm} = 25 \text{ m/s}$, substituting the value:

$v_{top} = 2 \times 25 = 50 \text{ m/s}$

questions.q: A string is wrapped around the edge of a uniform disc, and its free end is attached to the ceiling. The disc descends, unwinding the string. Determine the downward acceleration of the disc.
questions.solution:
Let $M$ be the mass and $R$ be the radius of the uniform disc.

Let $a$ be the downward acceleration of the center of mass and $\alpha$ be the angular acceleration of the disc.

Since the string is attached to the ceiling and unwinds without slipping, the point of contact has zero acceleration, which gives the constraint equation:

$a = \alpha R$

The forces acting on the disc are its weight $Mg$ downwards and the tension $T$ upwards. The equation of translational motion is:

$Mg - T = Ma$

The torque about the center of mass is provided by the tension $T$. The equation of rotational motion is:

$T R = I \alpha$

For a uniform disc, the moment of inertia about its central axis is $I = \dfrac{1}{2} M R^2$. Substituting $I$ and $\alpha = \dfrac{a}{R}$ into the torque equation:

$T R = \left( \dfrac{1}{2} M R^2 \right) \left( $\dfrac{a}{R} \right)

$T = $\dfrac{1}{2}$M a$

Substituting the value of $T$ into the translational equation:

$Mg - $\dfrac{1}{2}$M a = Ma$

$Mg = $\dfrac{3}{2}$M a$

$a = $\dfrac{2g}{3}

questions.q: A sphere of mass $m$ rolls along a plane surface. Determine its kinetic energy at an instant when its centre travels with speed $v$.
questions.solution:
The total kinetic energy of a rolling body is the sum of its translational and rotational kinetic energies.

$K = K_{trans} + K_{rot}$

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

For a solid sphere, the moment of inertia about its centre of mass is $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mR^2$.

For pure rolling, the relation between linear speed and angular speed is $v = \omega R$, which implies $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$.

Substituting the values of $I$ and $\omega$ into the rotational kinetic energy term:

$K_{rot} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{2}{5}mR^2\right) \left(\dfrac{v}{R}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{5}mv^2$

Adding both kinetic energies:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{5}mv^2 = \dfrac{7}{10}mv^2$

Since the ball rolls without slipping, the linear speed $v$ and angular speed $\omega$ are related by $v = \omega r$.

Substituting $I$ and $\omega$ into the energy equation:

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{2}{5}mr^2\right) \left(\dfrac{v}{r}\right)^2$

questions.q: A sphere begins rolling down an incline with an inclination $\theta$. Determine the speed of its centre once it has travelled a distance $l$.
questions.solution:

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

For pure rolling, $v = \omega R$.

questions.q: A hollow sphere is released from the top of an inclined plane of inclination $\theta$. Determine the minimum coefficient of friction between the sphere and the plane required to prevent sliding. Furthermore, find the kinetic energy of the ball as it travels down a length $l$ on the incline if the friction coefficient is half of this calculated minimum value.
questions.solution:
For a hollow sphere, the moment of inertia is $I = \dfrac{2}{3}mR^2$.

Let $a$ be the linear acceleration and $\alpha$ be the angular acceleration. For pure rolling, $a = \alpha R$.

The equations of motion are:
$mg\sin\theta - f = ma$
$fR = I\alpha = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}mR^2\right)\left(\dfrac{a}{R}\right) \Rightarrow f = \dfrac{2}{3}ma$

Substituting $f$ in the first equation:
$mg\sin\theta - \dfrac{2}{3}ma = ma \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{3}{5}g\sin\theta$

The required friction for pure rolling is:
$f = \dfrac{2}{3}m\left(\dfrac{3}{5}g\sin\theta\right) = \dfrac{2}{5}mg\sin\theta$

To prevent sliding, $f \le \mu N$, where $N = mg\cos\theta$:
$\dfrac{2}{5}mg\sin\theta \le \mu mg\cos\theta \Rightarrow \mu \ge \dfrac{2}{5}\tan\theta$

Thus, the minimum coefficient of friction is $\mu_\min = \dfrac{2}{5}\tan\theta$.

If the friction coefficient is half of this minimum value, $\mu = \dfrac{1}{5}\tan\theta$. The sphere will slide while rolling, and kinetic friction acts on it:
$f_k = \mu N = \left(\dfrac{1}{5}\tan\theta\right)(mg\cos\theta) = \dfrac{1}{5}mg\sin\theta$

The new linear acceleration $a'$ is:
$mg\sin\theta - f_k = ma' \Rightarrow a' = g\sin\theta - \dfrac{1}{5}g\sin\theta = \dfrac{4}{5}g\sin\theta$

The translational kinetic energy after traveling a distance $l$ is:
$K_t = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = ma'l = m\left(\dfrac{4}{5}g\sin\theta\right)l = \dfrac{4}{5}mgl\sin\theta$

The angular acceleration $\alpha'$ is:
$\alpha' = \dfrac{f_k R}{I} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{5}mgR\sin\theta}{\dfrac{2}{3}mR^2} = \dfrac{3g\sin\theta}{10R}$

The time $t$ taken to travel distance $l$ is given by $l = \dfrac{1}{2}a't^2$:
$t^2 = \dfrac{2l}{a'} = \dfrac{2l}{\dfrac{4}{5}g\sin\theta} = \dfrac{5l}{2g\sin\theta}$

The rotational kinetic energy after distance $l$ is:
$K_r = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}I(\alpha' t)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{2}{3}mR^2\right)\left(\dfrac{3g\sin\theta}{10R}\right)^2 \left(\dfrac{5l}{2g\sin\theta}\right)

$K_r = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}$mR^2\$right)\left(\dfrac{9g^2\sin^2\theta}{100R^2}\right)\left(\dfrac{5l}{2g\sin\theta}\right) = \dfrac{3}{40}$mgl\sin\theta$

The total kinetic energy is:
$K = K_t + K_r = $\dfrac{4}{5}$mgl\sin\theta + $\dfrac{3}{40}$mgl\$sin\theta = $\dfrac{35}{40}mgl\$sin\theta = \dfrac{7}{8}$mgl\$sin\theta

questions.q: A solid sphere of mass $m$ is released from rest at the rim of a hemispherical cup such that it rolls down the surface. Given that the rim of the hemisphere is kept horizontal, determine the normal force exerted by the cup on the ball as it reaches the bottom.
questions.solution:
Let $R$ be the radius of the hemispherical cup and $r$ be the radius of the solid sphere.

As the sphere rolls down from the rim to the bottom, its center of mass descends by a height $h = R - r$.

By conservation of mechanical energy, the loss in potential energy is equal to the gain in translational and rotational kinetic energy:

$mg(R - r) = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

For a solid sphere, the moment of inertia about its center of mass is $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2$. For pure rolling, the velocity of the center of mass is $v = \omega r$.

Substituting these values into the energy equation:

$mg(R - r) = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{5}mr^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{r}\right)^2$

$mg(R - r) = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{5}mv^2 = \dfrac{7}{10}mv^2$

From this, we can find the centripetal term:

$\dfrac{mv^2}{R - r} = \dfrac{10}{7}mg$

At the lowest point, the center of mass of the sphere moves in a circular path of radius $R - r$. The net force towards the center of the path provides the centripetal force:

$N - mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{R - r}$

Substituting the value of the centripetal term:

$N - mg = \dfrac{10}{7}mg$

$N = mg + \dfrac{10}{7}mg = \dfrac{17mg}{7}$

questions.q: As depicted in the figure, a rough track features a portion shaped like a cylinder of radius $R$. Find the minimum linear speed at which a sphere of radius $r$ should be set rolling on the horizontal segment so that it completely traverses the circle on the cylindrical part.
questions.solution:
For the sphere to completely traverse the circular track, it must not lose contact at the highest point. At the highest point, the minimum required speed $v_{top}$ is obtained when the normal force is zero.

The equation of motion for the center of mass at the highest point is:
$mg = \dfrac{mv_{top}^2}{R - r} \Rightarrow v_{top}^2 = g(R - r)$

The kinetic energy of a rolling solid sphere is:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{5}mr^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{r}\right)^2 = \dfrac{7}{10}mv^2$

The height of the center of the sphere at the highest point relative to its initial height is $h = 2(R - r)$.

Applying the principle of conservation of mechanical energy between the initial horizontal segment and the highest point of the circular track:

$K_{initial} = K_{top} + \Delta U$

$\dfrac{7}{10}mv_0^2 = \dfrac{7}{10}mv_{top}^2 + mgh$

Substituting $v_{top}^2 = g(R - r)$ and $h = 2(R - r)$:

$\dfrac{7}{10}mv_0^2 = \dfrac{7}{10}mg(R - r) + mg(2(R - r))$

$\dfrac{7}{10}v_0^2 = \left(\dfrac{7}{10} + 2\right)g(R - r)$

$\dfrac{7}{10}v_0^2 = \dfrac{27}{10}g(R - r)$

$v_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{27}{7}g(R - r)}$

questions.q: As shown in the figure, a small spherical ball of mass $m$ rolls down a loop track. The ball is released on the linear portion at a vertical height $H$ from the lowest point. The circular part shown has a radius $R$. Determine the kinetic energy of the ball when it is at a point $A$, where the radius makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal.
questions.solution:
Let the lowest point of the loop track be the reference level for zero gravitational potential energy ($U = 0$).

The ball is released from rest at a vertical height $H$. Therefore, its initial kinetic energy is zero, and its initial mechanical energy is entirely potential:
$E_i = mgH$

At point A, the radius of the circular track makes an angle $ heta$ with the horizontal. The center of the circular loop is at a height $R$ from the lowest point. The vertical height of point A from the center of the loop is $R\sin\theta$.
Thus, the total height of point A from the lowest point is:
$h_A = R + R\sin\theta$

The potential energy of the ball at point A is:
$U_A = mgh_A = mg(R + R\sin\theta)$

Since the ball rolls down the track, the point of contact is instantaneously at rest, meaning the static friction does no work. Therefore, the total mechanical energy of the system is conserved.

Let $K_A$ be the total kinetic energy of the ball at point A. By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy:
$E_i = U_A + K_A$

Substituting the values, we get:
$mgH = mg(R + R\sin\theta) + K_A$

Solving for the total kinetic energy $K_A$:
$K_A = mgH - mg(R + R\sin\theta)$
$K_A = mg(H - R - R\sin\theta)$

Note: The total kinetic energy is simply the loss in potential energy. If the question had specifically asked for the *translational* kinetic energy, it would be $\dfrac{5}{7}mg(H - R - R\sin\theta)$, but "kinetic energy" of a rolling body refers to its total kinetic energy (translational + rotational).

Answer: $mg(H - R - R\sin\theta)$

questions.q: A small spherical ball of mass $m$ rolls down a loop track. The ball is released on the linear portion at a vertical height $H$ from the lowest point. The circular part shown has a radius $R$. Determine the radial and the tangential accelerations of the centre when the ball is at a point $A$, where the radius makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. (Take the direction of velocity at $A$ as the positive tangential direction).
questions.solution:
Let the lowest point of the track be the reference level for potential energy. The height of point $A$ from the lowest point is $h = R + R\sin\theta$.

By conservation of mechanical energy, the loss in potential energy of the ball is equal to its gain in kinetic energy. For a solid sphere rolling without slipping, the total kinetic energy is the sum of translational and rotational kinetic energies:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

Substituting $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2$ and $\omega = \dfrac{v}{r}$:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{5}mr^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{r}\right)^2 = \dfrac{7}{10}mv^2$

Equating the loss in potential energy to the kinetic energy:

$mg(H - h) = \dfrac{7}{10}mv^2$

$mg(H - R - R\sin\theta) = \dfrac{7}{10}mv^2$

$v^2 = \dfrac{10}{7}g(H - R - R\sin\theta)$

The radial acceleration $a_r$ of the centre of the ball is given by $\dfrac{v^2}{R}$ (assuming the radius of the ball $r \ll R$):

$a_r = \dfrac{v^2}{R} = \dfrac{10}{7}g \left(\dfrac{H}{R} -$1 - \sin$\theta\right)

To find the tangential acceleration $a_t$, we can differentiate the velocity equation with respect to time $t$. Differentiating $v^2$ gives:

$2v $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{10}{7}$g \left(-R\cos\theta \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}\right)$

Since the tangential velocity is $v = R\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$ and tangential acceleration is $a_t = \dfrac{dv}{dt}$, we can substitute these into the equation:

$2v a_t = -\dfrac{10}{7}g\cos\theta \cdot v$

$a_t = -\dfrac{5}{7}g\cos\theta$

Thus, the radial and tangential accelerations are $\dfrac{10}{7}g \left(\dfrac{H}{R} -$1 - \sin$\theta\right) and $-$\dfrac{5}{7}$g\cos$\theta respectively.

Answer: Radial: \dfrac{10}{7}$g \left(\dfrac{H}{R} - 1 - \sin\theta\right)$, Tangential: $-\dfrac{5}{7}g\cos\theta$

questions.q: A small spherical ball of mass $m$ rolls down a loop track. The ball is released on the linear portion at a vertical height $H$ from the lowest point. The circular part shown has a radius $R$. Evaluate the normal force and the frictional force acting on the ball if $H = 60 \text{ cm}$, $R = 10 \text{ cm}$, $\theta = 0$ and $m = 70 \text{ g}$.
questions.solution:
Let the horizontal position on the loop track correspond to $\theta = 0$. At this point, the ball is at a height $R$ from the lowest point.

By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy from the release point to the horizontal position:

$mgH = mgR + \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

For a solid spherical ball, the moment of inertia is $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2$. For rolling without slipping, $v = \omega r$. Substituting these into the energy equation:

$mg(H - R) = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{5}mr^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{r}\right)^2$

$mg(H - R) = \dfrac{7}{10}mv^2 \Rightarrow v^2 = \dfrac{10}{7}g(H - R)$

The normal force $N$ at the horizontal position provides the necessary centripetal force:

$N = \dfrac{mv^2}{R} = \dfrac{10}{7}mg \left(\dfrac{H - R}{R}\right)

Given $m = 70 $\text{ g} =$0.07 $\text{ kg}, $g = 9.8 $\text{ m/s}^2$, $H = 60 $\text{ cm} =$0.6 $\text{ m}, and $R = 10 $\text{ cm} =$0.1 $\text{ m}:

$N = $\dfrac{10}{7} \times$0.07 $\times$9.8 $\times \left(\dfrac{0.6 - 0.1}{0.1}\right) =$0.1 $\times$9.8 $\times$5 = 4.9 $\text{ N}

To find the frictional force $f$, we analyze the tangential motion. Let $f$ act in the upward direction. The downward tangential force is gravity $mg$. The equation of linear motion is:

$mg - f = ma_t$

The torque about the center of mass is provided by the frictional force, which causes angular deceleration:

$\tau = f r = I$\alpha = \left(\dfrac{2}{5}mr^2\right)\left(\dfrac{a_t}{r}\right) \Rightarrowf = \dfrac{2}{5}ma_t \Rightarrow ma_t = \dfrac{5}{2}f$

Substituting $ma_t$ into the linear motion equation:

$mg - f = \dfrac{5}{2}f \Rightarrow \dfrac{7}{2}f = mg \Rightarrow f = \dfrac{2}{7}mg$

Calculating the magnitude of the frictional force:

$f = \dfrac{2}{7} \times0.07 \times9.8 = 0.02 \times9.8 = 0.196 \text{ N}$

Since the calculated value of $f$ is positive, the assumed upward direction is correct. The friction acts upward to provide the torque required to slow down the ball's rotation as it ascends.

Answer: $4.9 \text{ N},0.196 \text{ N}upward

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin spherical shell of radius $R$, resting on a rough horizontal surface, is struck sharply and horizontally by a cue. Where should it be struck so that the shell does not slip on the surface?
questions.solution:
Let the impulse applied by the cue be $J$ at a height $h$ above the centre of the thin spherical shell of mass $M$ and radius $R$.

The linear velocity $v$ acquired by the centre of mass is given by the linear impulse:

$J = Mv$

The angular velocity $\omega$ acquired by the shell is given by the angular impulse about the centre of mass:

$Jh = I\omega$

For a thin spherical shell, the moment of inertia about its diameter is $I = \dfrac{2}{3}MR^2$.

For the shell to not slip on the surface immediately after being struck, the velocity of the point of contact with the ground must be zero, which requires pure rolling:

$v = \omega R$

Substituting $v = \dfrac{J}{M}$ and $\omega = \dfrac{Jh}{I}$ into the pure rolling condition:

$\dfrac{J}{M} = \left(\dfrac{Jh}{\dfrac{2}{3}MR^2}\right)R$

$\dfrac{J}{M} = \dfrac{3Jh}{2MR}$

$1 = \dfrac{3h}{2R}$

$h = \dfrac{2R}{3}$

Thus, the shell should be struck at a height $\dfrac{2R}{3}$ above the centre.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform wheel of radius $R$ is made to rotate about its axis at an angular speed $\omega$. The rotating wheel is then placed on a rough horizontal surface, keeping its axis horizontal. Due to friction at the point of contact, the wheel accelerates forward while its rotational speed decreases until pure rolling begins. Determine the linear speed of the wheel once it achieves pure rolling.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the uniform wheel be $m$. A uniform wheel is considered as a uniform disc, so its moment of inertia about its central axis is $I = \dfrac{1}{2}mR^2$.

When the rotating wheel is placed on the rough horizontal surface, the frictional force acts at the point of contact. The normal reaction and gravitational force pass through the center of mass and are equal and opposite. Therefore, the net torque about any point on the ground along the line of motion is zero, and the angular momentum of the wheel about the point of contact is conserved.

Initial angular momentum about the point of contact:
$L_i = I\omega = \dfrac{1}{2}mR^2\omega$

Let $v$ be the linear speed and $\omega'$ be the angular speed when pure rolling begins. For pure rolling, $v = \omega' R$.

Final angular momentum about the point of contact:
$L_f = I\omega' + m v R = \dfrac{1}{2}mR^2\omega' + m(\omega' R)R = \dfrac{3}{2}mR^2\omega'$

By conservation of angular momentum ($L_i = L_f$):
$\dfrac{1}{2}mR^2\omega = \dfrac{3}{2}mR^2\omega'$

$\omega' = \dfrac{\omega}{3}$

The linear speed of the wheel is:
$v = \omega' R = \dfrac{\omega R}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin spherical shell resting on a rough horizontal surface is struck by a cue such that the line of action passes through the shell's centre. Consequently, the shell begins translating with a linear speed $v$ and zero initial angular velocity. Determine the linear speed of the shell once it commences pure rolling on the surface.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the thin spherical shell be $m$ and its radius be $R$.

The moment of inertia of the shell about its center is $I = \dfrac{2}{3}mR^2$.

Initially, the shell has a linear velocity $v$ and zero angular velocity. The angular momentum of the shell about any point on the horizontal surface is conserved because the frictional force passes through the surface (exerting zero torque) and the torques due to the normal reaction and weight cancel each other.

Initial angular momentum about a point on the surface is:

$L_i = m v R$

Let $v'$ be the linear speed and $\omega$ be the angular speed when pure rolling commences. For pure rolling, $v' = \omega R$.

Final angular momentum about the same point is:

$L_f = I \omega + m v' R$

Substituting $I = \dfrac{2}{3}mR^2$ and $\omega = \dfrac{v'}{R}$:

$L_f = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}mR^2\right) \left(\dfrac{v'}{R}\right) + m v' R = \dfrac{5}{3}m v' R$

By conservation of angular momentum, $L_i = L_f$:

$m v R = \dfrac{5}{3}m v' R$

$v' = \dfrac{3v}{5}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hollow sphere of radius $R$ rests on a smooth horizontal surface. It is pulled by a horizontal force acting tangentially at the highest point. Determine the distance travelled by the sphere during the time it completes one full rotation.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the hollow sphere be $m$ and the applied horizontal force be $F$.

The linear acceleration of the center of mass is given by Newton's second law:

$a = \dfrac{F}{m}$

The torque acting about the center of mass due to the force at the highest point is:

$\tau = F R$

The moment of inertia of a hollow sphere about its center of mass is $I = \dfrac{2}{3}mR^2$. The angular acceleration $\alpha$ is:

$\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I} = \dfrac{FR}{\dfrac{2}{3}mR^2} = \dfrac{3F}{2mR}$

Using the kinematic equations for linear and angular motion starting from rest, the distance travelled $s$ and the angular displacement $\theta$ in time $t$ are:

$s = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$

$\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$

Taking the ratio of $s$ to $\theta$:

$\dfrac{s}{\theta} = \dfrac{a}{\alpha} = \dfrac{\dfrac{F}{m}}{\dfrac{3F}{2mR}} = \dfrac{2R}{3}$

For one full rotation, the angular displacement is $\theta = 2\pi$. Substituting this into the ratio gives the distance travelled:

$s = \dfrac{2R}{3} \times 2\pi = \dfrac{4\pi R}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere of mass $0.50 \text{ kg}$ rests on a horizontal surface. The coefficient of static friction between the sphere and the surface is $2/7$. Determine the maximum horizontal force that can be applied at the highest point of the sphere such that it does not slip on the surface.
questions.solution:
Let the applied horizontal force at the highest point be $F$ and the force of static friction at the contact point be $f$, acting in the forward direction.

For translational motion, Newton's second law gives:
$F + f = ma$

For rotational motion about the center of mass, the torque equation is:
$F R - f R = I \alpha$

For a solid sphere, the moment of inertia is $I = \dfrac{2}{5} m R^2$. For pure rolling (no slipping), the acceleration of the center of mass is $a = \alpha R$.

Substituting these into the torque equation:
$F R - f R = $\$left(\dfrac{2}{5}$m R^2\right) \$left(\dfrac{a}{R}\right)
$F - f = $\dfrac{2}{5}$ma$

Now, we have a system of two equations:
1) $F + f = ma$
2) $F - f = $\dfrac{2}{5}$ma$

Adding the two equations:
$2F = $\dfrac{7}{5}$ma \Rightarrow ma = $\dfrac{10}{7}$F$

Substituting $ma$ back into the first equation to find $f$:
$F + f = $\dfrac{10}{7}$F \Rightarrow f = $\dfrac{3}{7}$F$

To prevent slipping, the static friction must not exceed its maximum possible value:
$f \le \mu_s N$
\dfrac{3}{7}$F \le \mu_s mg$

Solving for $F_\max$:
$F_\max = $\dfrac{7}{3} \mu_s mg$

Given $m = 0.50 \text{ kg}$, $\mu_s = $\dfrac{2}{7}, and taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:
$F_\max = $\dfrac{7}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{7} \times$0.50 \times 9.8$
$F_\max = $\dfrac{1}{3} \times$9.8 = 3.266... \text{ N}$

Rounding to two significant figures, we get $F_\max \approx 3.3 \text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As shown in the figure, a solid sphere is set into motion on a rough horizontal surface, possessing a forward linear speed $v$ and an anticlockwise angular speed $v/R$. Determine the linear speed of the sphere at the instant it stops rotating.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the solid sphere be $m$ and its radius be $R$. The moment of inertia of the solid sphere about its center of mass is $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mR^2$.

Consider a fixed point on the horizontal surface along the line of motion. The net torque about this point is zero because the line of action of the frictional force passes through the surface, and the torques due to the normal reaction and gravitational force cancel each other out.

Therefore, the angular momentum of the sphere about any fixed point on the ground is conserved.

Taking the clockwise direction as positive, the initial angular momentum due to translation is $mvR$ (clockwise) and due to rotation is $I\omega$ (anticlockwise).

Total initial angular momentum is:
$L_i = mvR - I\omega$

Substituting $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mR^2$ and $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$:
$L_i = mvR - \left(\dfrac{2}{5}mR^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{R}\right) = mvR - \dfrac{2}{5}mvR = \dfrac{3}{5}mvR$

Let $v'$ be the linear speed of the sphere at the instant it stops rotating. At this instant, its final angular velocity $\omega'$ is zero.

Total final angular momentum is:
$L_f = mv'R + I(0) = mv'R$

By conservation of angular momentum ($L_i = L_f$):
$\dfrac{3}{5}mvR = mv'R$

$v' = \dfrac{3v}{5}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere is set into motion on a rough horizontal surface, possessing a forward linear speed $v$ and an anticlockwise angular speed $v/R$. Determine the linear speed of the sphere at the moment slipping finally ceases and pure rolling begins.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the solid sphere be $m$ and its radius be $R$.

The initial linear velocity of the sphere is $v$ (forward) and its initial angular velocity is $\omega_0 = \dfrac{v}{R}$ (anticlockwise).

Taking the clockwise direction as positive, the initial angular momentum of the sphere about a fixed point on the ground is:

$L_i = m v R - I \omega_0$

Since the moment of inertia of a solid sphere is $I = \dfrac{2}{5} m R^2$, we have:

$L_i = m v R - \left(\dfrac{2}{5} m R^2\right) \left(\dfrac{v}{R}\right) = m v R - \dfrac{2}{5} m v R = \dfrac{3}{5} m v R$

Let the final linear velocity of the sphere when pure rolling begins be $v_f$. For pure rolling, the final angular velocity will be $\omega_f = \dfrac{v_f}{R}$ (clockwise).

The final angular momentum about the same point on the ground is:

$L_f = m v_f R + I \omega_f = m v_f R + \left(\dfrac{2}{5} m R^2\right) \left(\dfrac{v_f}{R}\right) = \dfrac{7}{5} m v_f R$

The frictional force acts at the point of contact, so its torque about any point on the ground is zero. The torques due to the normal force and gravity cancel each other. Thus, the net torque about the point on the ground is zero, and angular momentum is conserved:

$L_i = L_f$

$\dfrac{3}{5} m v R = \dfrac{7}{5} m v_f R$

$v_f = \dfrac{3v}{7}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere rolling on a rough horizontal surface with a linear speed $v$ elastically collides with a fixed, smooth, vertical wall. Determine the speed of the sphere after it commences pure rolling in the backward direction.
questions.solution:
Before the collision, the solid sphere is in pure rolling. Its linear velocity is $v$ and its angular velocity is $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$.

During the elastic collision with the smooth vertical wall, the linear velocity of the sphere reverses its direction, becoming $v$ in the backward direction. Since the wall is smooth, it exerts no torque about the center of mass, meaning the angular velocity remains unchanged in magnitude and direction.

Immediately after the collision, the sphere moves backward with speed $v$ but continues to rotate in the original direction with angular speed $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$.

Considering a point on the horizontal surface along the line of motion, the torque due to friction about this point is zero. Thus, the angular momentum of the sphere about this point is conserved.

Taking the backward direction as positive for linear velocity and the corresponding pure rolling rotation as positive for angular velocity, the initial angular momentum about the point on the ground is:

$L_i = m v R - I \omega$

Substituting $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mR^2$ and $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$:

$L_i = m v R - \left(\dfrac{2}{5}mR^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{R}\right) = \dfrac{3}{5}m v R$

Let $v_f$ be the final speed of the sphere when it commences pure rolling in the backward direction. The final angular velocity will be $\omega_f = \dfrac{v_f}{R}$. The final angular momentum about the same point is:

$L_f = m v_f R + I \omega_f = m v_f R + \left(\dfrac{2}{5}mR^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v_f}{R}\right) = \dfrac{7}{5}m v_f R$

By conservation of angular momentum, $L_i = L_f$:

$\dfrac{3}{5}m v R = \dfrac{7}{5}m v_f R$

$v_f = \dfrac{3v}{7}$
